Inference After Model Refutation:
Uniform Post-Relaxation Inference for Partially Identified Models

Ulrich Hounyo Affiliation: Department of Economics, University at Albany, State University of New York Email: khounyo@albany.edu
This version: November 11, 2026
Abstract

When data reject a model, the researcher must decide which identifying assumptions to give up. If several equally preferred repairs restore compatibility, the repair itself is unknown, and inference under any one of them can exclude structural values supported by the others. I propose Post-Relaxation Projection (PR), which carries one simultaneous confidence event through every repair that may be minimal. For a rectangular band on the repair-specific restrictions, PR contains exactly the post-relaxation targets compatible with that band. I also derive limits on learning the repair, its exact perturbation radius, oracle-equivalent adaptation, and versions for instrumental variables without a first-stage relevance bound. In cross-country data on institutions and income, the data do not settle which historical instrument to drop, yet every admissible minimum repair implies a positive effect, and the sign survives sizable direct effects of the instruments on income.

Keywords: model refutation; partial identification; sensitivity analysis; uniform inference; weak instruments.
JEL codes: C12; C14; C26.

1 Introduction

Empirical work rarely stops when a maintained model is rejected. The usual response is to weaken it: drop an exclusion restriction, remove a block of moment inequalities, or relax a shape or behavioral restriction. This step is innocuous when one relaxation is clearly the right one. It is not innocuous when several relaxations are judged equally costly on substantive grounds, each is just enough to restore compatibility with the data, and they support different values of the structural parameter. Choosing among them then changes the object being estimated, not only the estimator. In this paper each repair is a candidate relaxation written down before the sample is examined, the repairs are ranked by a scientific order fixed in advance, and the post-refutation target is built from every minimum feasible repair.

Let θ\theta denote the structural parameter, taking values in a compact set Θ\Theta, and let RR index a finite menu of repairs fixed before observing the sample. Repair RR has ex ante scientific cost c⁡(R)c(R) and identified set ΘR​(P)⊆Θ\Theta_{R}(P)\subseteq\Theta under the population distribution PP. Define

c⋆(P)=minR:ΘR​(P)≠∅c(R),ℛ⋆(P)={R:ΘR(P)≠∅,c(R)=c⋆(P)}.c^{\star}(P)=\min_{R:\Theta_{R}(P)\neq\varnothing}c(R),\qquad\mathcal{R}^{\star}(P)=\{R:\Theta_{R}(P)\neq\varnothing,\ c(R)=c^{\star}(P)\}.

When several repairs attain the minimum feasible cost, singling out one of them adds a restriction that the repair rule does not contain. The post-relaxation target is therefore

ΘM​R​(P)=⋃R∈ℛ⋆​(P)ΘR​(P).\boxed{\Theta^{MR}(P)=\bigcup_{R\in\mathcal{R}^{\star}(P)}\Theta_{R}(P).} (1)

The cost can encode equal deletion costs, unequal substantive priorities, or any other ranking chosen in advance, and Section 4.3 replaces it with any finite strict partial order. With two candidate instruments, for instance, if both equal-cost one-deletion repairs are feasible, both repair-specific identified sets belong to the target. In every case the target is conditional on the candidate restrictions and their ranking: the data determine which repairs are compatible with the population, not what a relaxation should cost.

The difficulty is that ℛ⋆​(P)\mathcal{R}^{\star}(P) is a discrete population object that has to be learned from the same data used for inference. Two populations that cannot be told apart at the usual local rates may have different minimum repairs and therefore different targets. Selecting a repair and then doing inference can fail even if the second step is exact, because the selection step may delete a whole component of the target. Throughout, fix 0<α<10<\alpha<1; Φ\Phi is the standard-normal cdf, z1−α=Φ−1​(1−α)z_{1-\alpha}=\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha), and ℙP\mathbb{P}_{P} denotes probability under PP.

A scalar example shows the problem. Two repairs have the same ex ante cost. The first always supports [1,2][1,2]. The second supports [m,0][m,0] when m≤0m\leq 0 and is infeasible when m>0m>0. At m=0m=0 both repairs are population-minimum, and the target, which I write ΘM​R​(m)\Theta^{MR}(m) in this example, is ΘM​R​(0)={0}∪[1,2]\Theta^{MR}(0)=\{0\}\cup[1,2]. Let Xi∼N⁡(m,1)X_{i}\sim N(m,1), X¯n=n−1​∑i=1nXi\bar{X}_{n}=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}, and suppose the researcher reports a single repair: the second when X¯n≤0\bar{X}_{n}\leq 0 and the first otherwise. Write ℙ0\mathbb{P}_{0} for probability at m=0m=0, and let CnhardC_{n}^{\mathrm{hard}} be the exact population identified set of the selected repair. There is no inferential error within the selected repair, yet

ℙ0{0∈Cnhard}=12,ℙ0{ΘM​R(0)⊆Cnhard}=0.\boxed{\mathbb{P}_{0}\{0\in C_{n}^{\mathrm{hard}}\}=\tfrac{1}{2},\qquad\mathbb{P}_{0}\{\Theta^{MR}(0)\subseteq C_{n}^{\mathrm{hard}}\}=0.} (2)

The first probability concerns the single value 00, the second the whole target. Selection loses 00 half of the time and, because the target is disconnected, never reports all of it. I call a repair boundary target-changing when crossing it adds values to ΘM​R​(P)\Theta^{MR}(P) or removes them. With several unresolved decisions, the probability of retaining a structural value is governed by a Gaussian carrier region (Section 3).

Information limits.

Two lower bounds describe what any procedure can achieve. A two-point argument bounds the minimax risk of estimating the minimum-repair correspondence. A local asymptotic normality (LAN) argument bounds how quickly an honest procedure can discard a value that belongs to the target at the boundary but drops out under a contiguous alternative. Let CnC_{n} be a confidence set and Pn,h​{⋅}P_{n,h}\{\cdot\} probability under the nn-sample local law indexed by hh, with h=0h=0 the boundary law. If θ†\theta^{\dagger} is such a value in the experiment of Assumption 2, with Fisher information II, then

lim infnPn,h{θ†∈Cn}≥Φ(z1−α−|h|I).\liminf_{n}P_{n,h}\{\theta^{\dagger}\in C_{n}\}\geq\Phi\!\left(z_{1-\alpha}-|h|\sqrt{I}\right). (3)

When the Gaussian membership region is convex, a simple exposed-face test attains this bound (Section 5). Finite unions of IV repairs need not be convex, and for them the bound can be far from attainable.

Uniform inference without learning the repair.

PR has no repair-selection step. Suppose repair RR has the primitive representation

ΘR(P)={θ∈Θ:bR​j(θ,P)≤0,j=1,…,KR},\Theta_{R}(P)=\{\theta\in\Theta:b_{Rj}(\theta,P)\leq 0,\ j=1,\ldots,K_{R}\},

with KR<∞K_{R}<\infty restrictions. A single simultaneous confidence event covers all these functions for all repairs. PR keeps every repair that, on this event, could still be population-minimum and takes the union of the corresponding structural outer sets. (“Projection” refers to carrying the event through the repair rule, not to a Euclidean projection.) On the event, every population-minimum repair and every value it supports are retained, so uniform coverage of the entire target needs neither consistent estimation of the optimal repair, nor of its active set, nor a derivative of the nonsmooth feasibility map.

When the feasibility bounds are computed from the same rectangular primitive band, the PR set is exactly the union of all post-relaxation targets compatible with that band (Theorem 4). No smaller set built from the realized band can contain the target for every compatible configuration, and the conclusions PR certifies are exactly those the band implies. This is a statement about the information in the band, not about statistical efficiency, and it can fail when repairs share primitives and that information is exploited (Remark 1). Section 4.3 also gives the exact sup-norm radius within which the minimal-repair correspondence cannot change.

PR sits between two familiar alternatives. Hard selection is too narrow near a target-changing boundary, as the example shows. The union over every repair in the menu is too wide, because it keeps costly relaxations that a cheaper feasible repair has made unnecessary; the same is true of taking the union of Anderson–Rubin or sensitivity sets computed repair by repair. Sensitivity analysis along a chosen path of relaxations does not account for sampling uncertainty about which discrete relaxation is minimal. PR keeps exactly the branches that the band cannot rule out as population-minimum. Section 9.5 compares these procedures in the application.

Coverage of the entire target also delivers conclusions shared by all minimum repairs. If the PR set lies inside a prespecified sign, threshold, or exclusion region, I say that the claim is certified. Any number of such claims can be read from the same event without a multiplicity correction, but near a target-changing boundary certifying a new claim is subject to the same local information limit as retaining a value.

Resolution and adaptation.

Broad protection is unnecessary once the repair configuration is well separated. Let ρn\rho_{n} be the stochastic resolution of the feasibility-index bounds and Δ⁡(P)\Delta(P) the distance to the nearest feasibility or minimality boundary. If Δ⁡(Pn)/ρn→∞\Delta(P_{n})/\rho_{n}\to\infty, PR recovers the minimum repairs with probability approaching one, and a version that certifies them on a small independent pilot sample is first-order equivalent to oracle inference that knows them.

Weak first stages.

In the IV model, uniformity need not rely on ratios of reduced-form coefficients. Let γj\gamma_{j} and πj\pi_{j} be the covariances of instrument jj with the outcome and with the endogenous regressor, after partialling out the controls. Pushing a simultaneous region for (γj,πj)j(\gamma_{j},\pi_{j})_{j} through the minimum-repair map with a single common witness gives a set that is uniformly valid without any lower bound on |πj||\pi_{j}|, including at πj=0\pi_{j}=0. When the first stages are nonzero but possibly weak, inverting Anderson–Rubin statistics instrument by instrument (Anderson and Rubin, 1949; Fieller, 1954) gives a sharper set. Simulations calibrated to the application show why this matters: with the weakest first stage at F≈10F\approx 10, as in the data, the regular ratio band covers only about 89%89\% of the time, whereas the score inversion stays at its nominal level.

Institutions application.

The application revisits the cross-country regressions of Rodrik, Subramanian, and Trebbi (2002; 2004), hereafter RST, and asks whether the positive effect of institutions on income survives uncertainty about which historical instrument should be abandoned. The tolerance rr bounds how far each instrument may depart from exact validity, in units of the structural coefficient. In the 80-country sample, where settler mortality and two language-based instruments are all available, the data cannot separate the seven repairs that keep at least one instrument. Even so, every band-compatible minimum-repair target is positive for every r∈[0,0.60]r\in[0,0.60] and every strictly positive additive deletion-cost vector, with or without a first-stage relevance bound. In RST’s 140-country sample only the two language instruments are available and Hansen’s test rejects their joint validity (p<0.01p<0.01). Dropping one or the other gives intervals that barely overlap, and the conventional estimate under the rejected model excludes part of each. PR keeps both repairs: its lower end, about 0.750.75, holds whichever instrument is dropped, while its upper end moves by about one unit of β\beta. With equal costs PR coincides in both samples with the union of the one-instrument intervals from the same band. The theory’s contribution there is to show that this union, rather than a selected repair or the uninformative structural bounds, is the honest report; the minimum-repair rule narrows it once the data certify a cheaper repair, which at the same estimates would take about three times as many countries and would then lift the lower bound at r=0.42r=0.42 from 0.460.46, the value for the union at that precision, to 0.870.87.

The tolerance has a direct economic reading: it bounds the direct effect of an instrument on income relative to its first stage. At the estimated first stages, the sign in the 80-country sample withstands direct effects of 0.200.20 to 0.260.26 log point of income per standard deviation of each instrument, all at once; for the English-language share this is two-thirds of its reduced-form association with income. Carrying the first-stage uncertainty through cuts the guaranteed protection to about 0.130.13 log point for the English-language share and to 0.040.04–0.050.05 for the other two instruments, whose first stages the data cannot bound well away from zero. The evidence for the sign therefore rests mainly on the language instrument with the strongest first stage. Across both samples, a move across the interquartile range of the rule-of-law index raises log income by at least about half of the interquartile income gap when the instruments are held to exact validity; whether institutions account for all of the gap depends on which historical identifying argument one trusts. All of these statements are conditional on the prespecified repair menu and on relaxing as little as necessary.

Relation to existing work.

The target builds on work on falsification and minimal relaxation. Masten and Poirier (2021) study the falsification frontier of continuous relaxations, and Li et al. (2024) take unions of identified sets across inclusion-minimal discrete relaxations; in the finite, compact setting of this paper, partial-order PR provides inference for that union. Apfel and Windmeijer (2024) extend the falsification-adaptive set to instruments that may violate either exclusion or conditional exogeneity. Sensitivity analysis studies how conclusions move along specified relaxations (Conley et al., 2012; Masten and Poirier, 2026); here sampling uncertainty also decides which discrete relaxation enters the target. The problem differs from set inference under a maintained model and from local misspecification (Chernozhukov et al., 2007; Andrews and Soares, 2010; Bugni et al., 2012; Andrews and Kwon, 2024). Constructions that maximize over a confidence set for a nuisance parameter are closer in spirit (Berger and Boos, 1994; Romano et al., 2014; McCloskey, 2017), but there the unresolved nuisance does not change the target. The failure of select-then-infer is related to the post-model-selection problem of Leeb and Pötscher (2005); the difference is that selection here changes the estimand, not only the sampling distribution of the estimator. Finally, Bei (2025) studies inference on union bounds whose index set is known; in the present problem the index set is the minimum-repair correspondence and must itself be learned.

Outline.

Section 2 describes the population geometry of minimum repair, Section 3 the local limits, Section 4 the PR procedure, Section 5 the Gaussian benchmark, and Section 6 resolution-adaptive inference. Section 7 specializes to instrumental variables, Section 8 reports simulations, and Section 9 the application. Proofs, the IV calibration theory, and additional empirical material are in the Appendix.

2 Population Minimum Repair

Let (𝒫,d𝒫)(\mathcal{P},d_{\mathcal{P}}) be a metric space of distributions, let (Θ,dΘ)(\Theta,d_{\Theta}) be a nonempty compact metric parameter space, and let ℛ\mathcal{R} be a finite collection of admissible repairs. Each repair R∈ℛR\in\mathcal{R} has fixed ex ante cost c⁡(R)c(R) and identified set ΘR​(P)⊆Θ\Theta_{R}(P)\subseteq\Theta. For θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta and A,B⊆ΘA,B\subseteq\Theta, write dist⁡{θ,B}=infb∈BdΘ​(θ,b)\dist\{\theta,B\}=\inf_{b\in B}d_{\Theta}(\theta,b), dist⁡(A,B)=infa∈A,b∈BdΘ​(a,b)\dist(A,B)=\inf_{a\in A,b\in B}d_{\Theta}(a,b), and e⁡(A,B)=supa∈Adist⁡{a,B}e(A,B)=\sup_{a\in A}\dist\{a,B\} for the directed excess of AA over BB, with dist⁡{θ,∅}=dist⁡(A,∅)=+∞\dist\{\theta,\varnothing\}=\dist(A,\varnothing)=+\infty and e⁡(∅,B)=0e(\varnothing,B)=0. For compact sets, possibly empty, dH​(A,B)=max⁡{e⁡(A,B),e⁡(B,A)}d_{H}(A,B)=\max\{e(A,B),e(B,A)\} is the extended Hausdorff distance; it is the ordinary one for nonempty sets, and dH​(A,∅)=+∞d_{H}(A,\varnothing)=+\infty for A≠∅A\neq\varnothing.

Assumption 1 (Population repair geometry).

For every P∈𝒫P\in\mathcal{P}: (i) at least one repair is feasible; (ii) each repair has a continuous feasibility index qR:𝒫→ℝq_{R}:\mathcal{P}\to\mathbb{R} satisfying ΘR​(P)≠∅\Theta_{R}(P)\neq\varnothing if and only if qR​(P)≤0q_{R}(P)\leq 0; and (iii) the correspondence P↦ΘR​(P)P\mapsto\Theta_{R}(P) has sequentially closed graph. The repair collection is finite, costs are fixed ex ante, and Θ\Theta is compact.

When each repair has the primitive representation of Section 4.1, continuity of the primitive functions in θ\theta together with their uniform convergence along convergent sequences of distributions implies part (iii), and with the canonical index of that section also part (ii) (Appendix, Lemma 2). PR coverage itself requires neither.

Define

ℱ⁡(P)={R∈ℛ:ΘR​(P)≠∅},c⋆​(P)=minR∈ℱ⁡(P)⁡c⁡(R),\mathcal{F}(P)=\{R\in\mathcal{R}:\Theta_{R}(P)\neq\varnothing\},\qquad c^{\star}(P)=\min_{R\in\mathcal{F}(P)}c(R),
ℛ⋆​(P)={R∈ℱ⁡(P):c⁡(R)=c⋆​(P)},ΘM​R​(P)=⋃R∈ℛ⋆​(P)ΘR​(P).\mathcal{R}^{\star}(P)=\{R\in\mathcal{F}(P):c(R)=c^{\star}(P)\},\qquad\Theta^{MR}(P)=\bigcup_{R\in\mathcal{R}^{\star}(P)}\Theta_{R}(P).

Because ℛ\mathcal{R} is finite and at least one repair is feasible (Assumption 1(i)), both c⋆​(P)c^{\star}(P) and ℛ⋆​(P)\mathcal{R}^{\star}(P) are well defined. Under Assumption 1(iii), each repair-specific set is closed in compact Θ\Theta; hence ΘM​R​(P)\Theta^{MR}(P) is nonempty and compact, so the Hausdorff distances used below are well defined.

If repairs are deletion sets and cost rises strictly with inclusion, as it does under positive additive deletion costs, every cost-minimum feasible repair is inclusion-minimal, but not conversely: two inclusion-minimal repairs may carry different costs. The cost-minimum target is the union over inclusion-minimal relaxations only when those share the minimum cost.

The finite-repair formulation is not specific to IV: it covers any finite collection of exclusion, moment, shape, sign, behavioral, or measurement restrictions that can be relaxed in prespecified blocks, provided each repaired model has the primitive representation of Section 4.

Theorem 1 (Population geometry of minimum repair).

Under Assumption 1:

  1. (i)

    c⋆​(P)c^{\star}(P) is lower semicontinuous.

  2. (ii)

    If some R∈ℛ⋆​(P0)R\in\mathcal{R}^{\star}(P_{0}) satisfies qR​(P0)<0q_{R}(P_{0})<0, then locally c⋆​(P)=c⋆​(P0)c^{\star}(P)=c^{\star}(P_{0}) and ℛ⋆​(P)⊆ℛ⋆​(P0)\mathcal{R}^{\star}(P)\subseteq\mathcal{R}^{\star}(P_{0}).

  3. (iii)

    If qR​(P0)<0q_{R}(P_{0})<0 for every R∈ℛ⋆​(P0)R\in\mathcal{R}^{\star}(P_{0}), then locally ℛ⋆​(P)=ℛ⋆​(P0)\mathcal{R}^{\star}(P)=\mathcal{R}^{\star}(P_{0}).

  4. (iv)

    Let Pn→P0P_{n}\to P_{0} and define ℰ={R:R∈ℛ⋆​(Pn)​ infinitely often}\mathscr{E}=\{R:R\in\mathcal{R}^{\star}(P_{n})\text{ infinitely often}\}. If θ†∈ΘM​R​(P0)\theta^{\dagger}\in\Theta^{MR}(P_{0}) but θ†∉ΘR​(P0)\theta^{\dagger}\notin\Theta_{R}(P_{0}) for every R∈ℰR\in\mathscr{E}, then there exist δ>0\delta>0 and N<∞N<\infty such that

    dist⁡{θ†,ΘM​R​(Pn)}≥δ∀n≥N.\dist\{\theta^{\dagger},\Theta^{MR}(P_{n})\}\geq\delta\qquad\forall n\geq N.

    Consequently,

    lim infn→∞dH​{ΘM​R​(Pn),ΘM​R​(P0)}≥δ>0.\liminf_{n\to\infty}d_{H}\{\Theta^{MR}(P_{n}),\Theta^{MR}(P_{0})\}\geq\delta>0.

Parts (i)–(iii) say that strict feasibility stabilizes both the minimum cost and the repair correspondence. Part (iv) describes the mechanism by which the target can jump; it does not classify all discontinuities. Its proof uses finiteness of the menu to find a repair that is minimal infinitely often and graph closedness to pass membership to the limit. Compactness of Θ\Theta makes the repair-specific sets and their finite union compact, and repairability keeps the target nonempty.

Definition 1 (Target-changing repair boundary).

A distribution P0P_{0} is a target-changing repair boundary if there exist a sequence Pn→P0P_{n}\to P_{0}, a value θ†∈ΘM​R​(P0)\theta^{\dagger}\in\Theta^{MR}(P_{0}), and δ>0\delta>0 such that

dist⁡{θ†,ΘM​R​(Pn)}≥δ\dist\{\theta^{\dagger},\Theta^{MR}(P_{n})\}\geq\delta

for all sufficiently large nn, and the jump is not generated by an ordinary discontinuity of a repair-specific set that remains feasible. Formally, for every repair RR with ΘR​(P0)≠∅\Theta_{R}(P_{0})\neq\varnothing and every subsequence nkn_{k} on which ΘR​(Pnk)≠∅\Theta_{R}(P_{n_{k}})\neq\varnothing,

dH​{ΘR​(Pnk),ΘR​(P0)}→0.d_{H}\{\Theta_{R}(P_{n_{k}}),\Theta_{R}(P_{0})\}\to 0.

The extra continuity clause isolates changes attributable to the feasibility or minimality status of a repair rather than to a discontinuity inside a fixed feasible repaired model. Theorem 1(iv) supplies the separation; the continuity clause is what justifies calling the jump a repair boundary.

Two feasible repairs of equal cost both belong to ℛ⋆​(P)\mathcal{R}^{\star}(P), however negative their feasibility indices; qRq_{R} records feasibility and is not a secondary ranking. The nonregular event is therefore a repair becoming feasible or infeasible.

3 Repair Uncertainty and Local Adaptation

Three criteria recur below and should be kept apart. For an estimator ℛ^n\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{n} of the minimum-repair correspondence, repair recovery concerns ℙP{ℛ^n=ℛ⋆(P)}\mathbb{P}_{P}\{\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{n}=\mathcal{R}^{\star}(P)\}, entire-target coverage concerns ℙP{ΘM​R(P)⊆Cn}\mathbb{P}_{P}\{\Theta^{MR}(P)\subseteq C_{n}\}, and structural-value coverage concerns ℙP{θ∈Cn}\mathbb{P}_{P}\{\theta\in C_{n}\} for θ∈ΘM​R​(P)\theta\in\Theta^{MR}(P). PR targets entire-target coverage, the Gaussian adaptation problem studies structural-value coverage, and learning the repair correspondence is a classification problem. Confidence procedures are measurable random closed subsets of Θ\Theta, or measurable acceptance rules in the Gaussian limit experiment, so all coverage events below are well defined.

3.1 Two-point repair classification

Let Pn,0P_{n,0} and Pn,1P_{n,1} denote two sequences of local distributions whose population-minimum repair correspondences differ. For an estimator ℛ^n\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{n}, let

en,j=Pn,jn{ℛ^n≠ℛ⋆(Pn,j)},j=0,1.e_{n,j}=P_{n,j}^{n}\{\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{n}\neq\mathcal{R}^{\star}(P_{n,j})\},\qquad j=0,1.

For probability laws PP and QQ, write ‖P−Q‖T​V=supA|P⁡(A)−Q⁡(A)|\|P-Q\|_{TV}=\sup_{A}|P(A)-Q(A)| for their total-variation distance.

Theorem 2 (Repair classification).

The minimax risk of estimating the population-minimum repair correspondence satisfies

infℛ^nmax⁡{en,0,en,1}≥1−‖Pn,0n−Pn,1n‖T​V2.\inf_{\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{n}}\max\{e_{n,0},e_{n,1}\}\geq\frac{1-\|P_{n,0}^{n}-P_{n,1}^{n}\|_{TV}}{2}. (4)

𝔊n={𝒟⊆ℛ:θn†∈Θ𝒟​(Pn)}.\mathfrak{G}_{n}=\{\mathcal{D}\subseteq\mathcal{R}:\theta_{n}^{\dagger}\in\Theta_{\mathcal{D}}(P_{n})\}.

If, in an isolated-boundary experiment, the asymptotic carrier event is {Z≤0}\{Z\leq 0\} with Z∼N⁡(0,1)Z\sim N(0,1) and all other repair decisions are separated, the bound in (8) converges to 1/21/2. More generally, with several unresolved Gaussian decisions it converges to the probability of the corresponding carrier region, which equals 2−k2^{-k} only when the region is the negative orthant of kk independent standard normal decisions.

The corollary separates repair-selection failure from within-repair inference error. A procedure can estimate one repair label accurately and still miss the post-relaxation target when another same-cost minimum repair carries structural values absent from the selected target.

3.2 The local adaptation problem

Suppose a value θ†\theta^{\dagger} belongs to the boundary target and disappears under a contiguous alternative. The confidence procedure faces a one-sided testing problem: exclusion of θ†\theta^{\dagger} is a rejection of the boundary state.

Assumption 2 (Regular LAN boundary).

Along a scalar local submodel {Pn,h:h∈ℝ}⊂𝒫\{P_{n,h}:h\in\mathbb{R}\}\subset\mathcal{P}, for every fixed h∈ℝh\in\mathbb{R}, let Pn,hnP_{n,h}^{n} denote the nn-sample law and abbreviate probability under it by Pn,h​{⋅}P_{n,h}\{\cdot\}. Use oPn,0​(1)o_{P_{n,0}}(1) for convergence in probability under Pn,0nP_{n,0}^{n}. Then

log⁡d​Pn,hnd​Pn,0n=h​ζn−12​h2​I+oPn,0​(1),ζn⇒N⁡(0,I),\log\frac{dP_{n,h}^{n}}{dP_{n,0}^{n}}=h\zeta_{n}-\frac{1}{2}h^{2}I+o_{P_{n,0}}(1),\qquad\zeta_{n}\Rightarrow N(0,I),

with 0<I<∞0<I<\infty.

Theorem 3 (Local adaptation lower bound).

Suppose Assumption 2 holds and θ†∈ΘM​R​(Pn,0)\theta^{\dagger}\in\Theta^{MR}(P_{n,0}) for all sufficiently large nn. If

lim infnPn,0{ΘM​R(Pn,0)⊆Cn}≥1−α,\liminf_{n}P_{n,0}\{\Theta^{MR}(P_{n,0})\subseteq C_{n}\}\geq 1-\alpha,

then for every fixed hh,

lim infnPn,h{θ†∈Cn}≥Φ[z1−α−|h|I].\liminf_{n}P_{n,h}\{\theta^{\dagger}\in C_{n}\}\geq\Phi\!\left[z_{1-\alpha}-|h|\sqrt{I}\right]. (9)

If, additionally, for some δ>0\delta>0, dist⁡{θ†,ΘM​R​(Pn,h)}≥δ\dist\{\theta^{\dagger},\Theta^{MR}(P_{n,h})\}\geq\delta eventually, then

lim infnPn,h{e(Cn,ΘM​R(Pn,h))≥δ}≥Φ[z1−α−|h|I].\liminf_{n}P_{n,h}\{e(C_{n},\Theta^{MR}(P_{n,h}))\geq\delta\}\geq\Phi\!\left[z_{1-\alpha}-|h|\sqrt{I}\right].

The proof is the usual LAN power-envelope argument; what the repair structure adds is the local paths along which the target changes through feasibility or minimality status while every repair-specific set stays well behaved (Definition 1). The scalar example of the introduction is such a path with I=1I=1. Appendix S4.1 gives an IV version with four instruments and equal deletion costs: two pairs of instruments are both feasible at the boundary, and a local move of one coefficient makes the second pair infeasible, so a component of the target at distance 10​r10r from the rest disappears. If that coefficient is estimated with asymptotic variance σ2\sigma^{2}, independently of the others, then I=σ−2I=\sigma^{-2}, and any honest procedure keeps the vanished component with probability at least Φ⁡(z1−α−|h|/σ)\Phi(z_{1-\alpha}-|h|/\sigma).

4 Uniform Post-Relaxation Projection

The construction retains the finite repair menu and fixed ex ante costs and assumes repairability: for every P∈𝒫P\in\mathcal{P}, at least one R∈ℛR\in\mathcal{R} satisfies ΘR​(P)≠∅\Theta_{R}(P)\neq\varnothing. Then c⋆​(P)c^{\star}(P), ℛ⋆​(P)\mathcal{R}^{\star}(P), and ΘM​R​(P)\Theta^{MR}(P) are all well defined. PR itself does not need continuity of P↦qR​(P)P\mapsto q_{R}(P) or sequentially closed repair graphs; those conditions were used only for the population stability result.

4.1 Primitive representation

For each repair RR, suppose

ΘR(P)={θ∈Θ:bR​j(θ,P)≤0,j=1,…,KR},\Theta_{R}(P)=\{\theta\in\Theta:b_{Rj}(\theta,P)\leq 0,\ j=1,\ldots,K_{R}\}, (10)

For a continuous array f=(f1,…,fKR)f=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{K_{R}}) on Θ\Theta, define bR​(P)=(bR​j​(⋅,P))j=1KRb_{R}(P)=(b_{Rj}(\cdot,P))_{j=1}^{K_{R}} and the canonical min–max map and its induced feasibility index by

QR​(f)=minθ∈Θ⁡max1≤j≤KR​fj​(θ),qRQ​(P)=QR​{bR​(P)}.Q_{R}(f)=\min_{\theta\in\Theta}\max_{1\leq j\leq K_{R}}f_{j}(\theta),\qquad q_{R}^{Q}(P)=Q_{R}\{b_{R}(P)\}. (11)

By compactness and continuity, qRQ​(P)≤0q_{R}^{Q}(P)\leq 0 if and only if ΘR​(P)≠∅\Theta_{R}(P)\neq\varnothing, and QRQ_{R} is coordinatewise monotone and one-Lipschitz in the sup norm, |QR​(f)−QR​(g)|≤‖f−g‖∞|Q_{R}(f)-Q_{R}(g)|\leq\|f-g\|_{\infty}.

PR does not require this particular scale. Any scalar qR​(P)q_{R}(P) with

qR(P)≤0⟺ΘR(P)≠∅q_{R}(P)\leq 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\Theta_{R}(P)\neq\varnothing (12)

is allowed; in the IV application of Section 7, qR=LR−URq_{R}=L_{R}-U_{R} is twice the canonical index when the structural bounds do not bind.

4.2 A simultaneous primitive and feasibility band

Assumption 3 (Common primitive-and-feasibility honesty).

For every R,jR,j, the random endpoints b¯R​j,n​(θ)\underline{b}_{Rj,n}(\theta) and b¯R​j,n​(θ)\overline{b}_{Rj,n}(\theta) are jointly measurable in the data and θ\theta, continuous in θ\theta almost surely, and satisfy b¯R​j,n​(θ)≤b¯R​j,n​(θ)\underline{b}_{Rj,n}(\theta)\leq\overline{b}_{Rj,n}(\theta) for all θ\theta almost surely. (13)

Assume

lim infninfP∈𝒫ℙP​{ℰn​(P)}≥1−α.\liminf_{n}\inf_{P\in\mathcal{P}}\mathbb{P}_{P}\{\mathcal{E}_{n}(P)\}\geq 1-\alpha. (14)

Here ℰn​(P)\mathcal{E}_{n}(P) is one joint event over all primitive and feasibility bounds; marginal coordinatewise coverage is not enough.

If qR=qRQq_{R}=q_{R}^{Q}, one valid construction is

q¯R,n=QR​(b¯R,n),q¯R,n=QR​(b¯R,n),\underline{q}_{R,n}=Q_{R}(\underline{b}_{R,n}),\qquad\overline{q}_{R,n}=Q_{R}(\overline{b}_{R,n}), (15)

because QRQ_{R} is monotone. Assumption 3 also permits sharper scalar bounds obtained directly from contrasts or exact algebra, as in the IV implementation below.

Repair RR is plausibly population-minimum when its own feasibility remains possible and no cheaper repair is known to be feasible:

ℜ^n={R:q¯R,n≤0,q¯S,n>0∀S:c(S)<c(R)}.\widehat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n}=\left\{R:\underline{q}_{R,n}\leq 0,\ \overline{q}_{S,n}>0\ \forall S:c(S)<c(R)\right\}. (16)

The strict inequality for cheaper repairs matters: if q¯S,n=0\overline{q}_{S,n}=0, cheaper repair SS is feasible throughout the coordinatewise box and every more costly repair is ruled out.

For each repair define the structural outer set

Cn,R={θ∈Θ:b¯R​j,n​(θ)≤0​∀j},C_{n,R}=\{\theta\in\Theta:\underline{b}_{Rj,n}(\theta)\leq 0\ \forall j\}, (17)

and let

CnPR=⋃R∈ℜ^nCn,R.C_{n}^{\mathrm{PR}}=\bigcup_{R\in\widehat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n}}C_{n,R}. (18)

The feasibility sandwich decides which branches remain possible, and the lower primitive band supplies the structural outer set on each retained branch; a retained branch with an empty outer set contributes nothing.

For the canonical construction, let 𝔅n\mathfrak{B}_{n} be the set of continuous primitive arrays f=(fR​j)f=(f_{Rj}) satisfying b¯R​j,n≤fR​j≤b¯R​j,n\underline{b}_{Rj,n}\leq f_{Rj}\leq\overline{b}_{Rj,n} pointwise. Define ΘR​(f)={θ:fR​j​(θ)≤0​∀j}\Theta_{R}(f)=\{\theta:f_{Rj}(\theta)\leq 0\ \forall j\} and qR​(f)=QR​(fR)q_{R}(f)=Q_{R}(f_{R}), let 𝔅nrep\mathfrak{B}_{n}^{\mathrm{rep}} contain the arrays with at least one feasible repair, and define T⁡(f)T(f) by the same minimum-cost union rule as ΘM​R​(P)\Theta^{MR}(P).

Theorem 4 (Bandwise completeness of canonical PR).

Suppose the scalar feasibility bounds are canonical as in (15). For every realization of the primitive rectangle,

CnPR=⋃f∈𝔅nrepT⁡(f).C_{n}^{\mathrm{PR}}=\bigcup_{f\in\mathfrak{B}_{n}^{\mathrm{rep}}}T(f). (19)

Hence any D⊆ΘD\subseteq\Theta satisfying T⁡(f)⊆DT(f)\subseteq D for every f∈𝔅nrepf\in\mathfrak{B}_{n}^{\mathrm{rep}} must contain CnPRC_{n}^{\mathrm{PR}}. Moreover, for every claim region A⊆ΘA\subseteq\Theta,

CnPR⊆A⟺T(f)⊆A∀f∈𝔅nrep.C_{n}^{\mathrm{PR}}\subseteq A\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T(f)\subseteq A\quad\forall f\in\mathfrak{B}_{n}^{\mathrm{rep}}. (20)

The same statements hold for any fixed finite strict partial order after replacing minimum-cost repairs by ≺\prec-minimal feasible repairs.

The result is conditional on the realized rectangle: canonical PR discards a value only when every primitive configuration permitted by the band excludes it. A smaller honest set must therefore use information that the rectangle does not record, such as restrictions linking the primitives of different repairs or a nonrectangular joint region. Separately supplied sharper feasibility bounds still deliver the coverage in Theorem 5, but the equality in (19) then requires a joint-compatibility condition.

Remark 1 (Shared primitives).

The set 𝔅n\mathfrak{B}_{n} lets the primitive bounds of different repairs move independently. When two repairs share a primitive function, as two IV repairs that retain the same instrument do, the honest information set is smaller, and canonical PR can be strictly larger than the union of targets compatible with it. For example, let Θ=[−1,2]\Theta=[-1,2], r=0.1r=0.1, let R0R_{0} retain both instruments (cost 00) and R1R_{1} only the first (cost 11), and let the band be β1∈[0,1]\beta_{1}\in[0,1], β2∈[0.10,0.15]\beta_{2}\in[0.10,0.15]. Repair by repair, R0R_{0} cannot be shown feasible, so R1R_{1} is retained and contributes [−0.1,1.1][-0.1,1.1]. If the same β1\beta_{1} must enter both repairs, a value θ<0\theta<0 requires β1<0.1\beta_{1}<0.1, hence |β1−β2|≤0.15<2​r|\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}|\leq 0.15<2r; then R0R_{0} is feasible and its target [β2−r,β1+r][\beta_{2}-r,\beta_{1}+r] lies in [0,∞)[0,\infty). Hence [−0.1,0)[-0.1,0) belongs to CnPRC_{n}^{\mathrm{PR}} but to no target compatible with the shared band, and the gap persists if the menu also contains the repair that keeps only the second instrument. Theorem 4 is therefore a sharpness result for the rectangular information set. Exploiting shared primitives requires a joint projection of the kind used in Section 7.4. In the simulation of Appendix S17, built on this configuration, the joint projection is shorter than PR in at most a fifth of the samples, and its average length is within one percent of PR’s.

For repair recovery, measure uncertainty in the scale that actually governs the repair rule:

ηn​(P)=maxR∈ℛ⁡max⁡{|q¯R,n−qR​(P)|,|q¯R,n−qR​(P)|}.\eta_{n}(P)=\max_{R\in\mathcal{R}}\max\left\{|\underline{q}_{R,n}-q_{R}(P)|,|\overline{q}_{R,n}-q_{R}(P)|\right\}. (21)
Assumption 4 (Statistical resolution rate).

There exists a deterministic sequence ρn↓0\rho_{n}\downarrow 0 such that

limM→∞lim supn→∞supP∈𝒫ℙP{ηn(P)>Mρn}=0.\lim_{M\to\infty}\limsup_{n\to\infty}\sup_{P\in\mathcal{P}}\mathbb{P}_{P}\{\eta_{n}(P)>M\rho_{n}\}=0. (22)

Define the population repair-resolution margin

Δ⁡(P)=min⁡(CLOSE\displaystyle\Delta(P)=\min\Big( {−qR​(P):R∈ℛ⋆​(P)}\displaystyle\{-q_{R}(P):R\in\mathcal{R}^{\star}(P)\}
∪{qS​(P):c⁡(S)<c⋆​(P)}\displaystyle\cup\{q_{S}(P):c(S)<c^{\star}(P)\}
∪{qS(P):c(S)=c⋆(P),S∉ℛ⋆(P)}),\displaystyle\cup\{q_{S}(P):c(S)=c^{\star}(P),\ S\notin\mathcal{R}^{\star}(P)\}\Big), (23)

with empty groups omitted. In particular, if a true minimum repair lies on its feasibility boundary, then Δ⁡(P)=0\Delta(P)=0. Since Δ\Delta and ηn\eta_{n} use the same scale, the recovery condition is unchanged by a common positive rescaling of all feasibility indices. Rescaling repairs by different factors does change Δ⁡(P)/ρn\Delta(P)/\rho_{n}; with indices on different scales, the condition should be read repair by repair, each margin against the resolution of its own index.

Under Assumption 3, CnPRC_{n}^{\mathrm{PR}} is a measurable random closed set (Appendix, Lemma 6).

The procedure in four steps.

For readers who want the computation before the theory:

  1. 1.

    List the repairs R∈ℛR\in\mathcal{R}, their costs (or a partial order), and for each repair the restrictions bR​j​(θ,P)≤0b_{Rj}(\theta,P)\leq 0, all fixed before seeing the data.

  2. 2.

    Compute one simultaneous (1−α)(1-\alpha) band for all primitive functions and all feasibility indices, giving b¯R​j,n≤b¯R​j,n\underline{b}_{Rj,n}\leq\overline{b}_{Rj,n} and q¯R,n≤q¯R,n\underline{q}_{R,n}\leq\overline{q}_{R,n}.

  3. 3.

    Keep repair RR if q¯R,n≤0\underline{q}_{R,n}\leq 0 and q¯S,n>0\overline{q}_{S,n}>0 for every cheaper SS; this is the set ℜ^n\widehat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n} in (16).

  4. 4.

    Report CnPR=⋃R∈ℜ^n{θ:b¯R​j,n​(θ)≤0​∀j}C_{n}^{\mathrm{PR}}=\bigcup_{R\in\widehat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n}}\{\theta:\underline{b}_{Rj,n}(\theta)\leq 0\ \forall j\}, and read off any conclusion that holds on the whole set.

All the statistical work is in step 2.

Theorem 5 (Uniform PR and repair recovery).

Under the primitive repair setup and Assumption 3, on ℰn​(P)\mathcal{E}_{n}(P),

ℛ⋆​(P)⊆ℜ^nandΘM​R​(P)⊆CnPR.\mathcal{R}^{\star}(P)\subseteq\widehat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\Theta^{MR}(P)\subseteq C_{n}^{\mathrm{PR}}.

Consequently,

lim infninfP∈𝒫ℙP{ΘM​R(P)⊆CnPR}≥1−α.\liminf_{n}\inf_{P\in\mathcal{P}}\mathbb{P}_{P}\{\Theta^{MR}(P)\subseteq C_{n}^{\mathrm{PR}}\}\geq 1-\alpha. (24)

If, in addition, Assumption 4 holds and a sequence Pn∈𝒫P_{n}\in\mathcal{P} satisfies

Δ⁡(Pn)/ρn→∞,\Delta(P_{n})/\rho_{n}\to\infty, (25)

then

ℙPn{ℜ^n=ℛ⋆(Pn)}→1.\mathbb{P}_{P_{n}}\{\widehat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n}=\mathcal{R}^{\star}(P_{n})\}\to 1. (26)

For recovery, a costlier false repair is blocked by a cheaper true minimum repair, whereas a same-cost infeasible repair is excluded when its own lower feasibility endpoint becomes positive. The latter is the third group in Δ⁡(P)\Delta(P) in (23).

Coverage and repair recovery answer different questions. Coverage (24) holds at a fixed level and does not require learning the repair; recovery (26) describes what happens under separation. In a regular fixed-dimensional problem ρn≍n−1/2\rho_{n}\asymp n^{-1/2}, so the repair correspondence becomes learnable only when the feasibility margins dominate root-nn uncertainty.

The inclusions in Theorem 5 are deterministic on ℰn​(P)\mathcal{E}_{n}(P), so PR inherits exactly the coverage of the simultaneous band: a finite-sample band gives finite-sample coverage, and no further resampling is needed once the band is available. Section 7 verifies the band uniformly for the IV class used here.

Theorem 4 compares PR only with sets that use the rectangular band. It is not a statement about the shortest honest set among all procedures, and PR need not attain the bound of Section 5.

4.3 Partial orders and the stability radius of the repair map

Scalar costs are convenient, but the projection argument does not need them. Let ≺\prec be a fixed strict partial order on the finite repair menu, chosen before observing the sample, where S≺RS\prec R means that repair SS is scientifically preferred to repair RR. The ex-ante qualification is essential: if the order were estimated from the same sample, uncertainty about the ranking would create another target-selection problem not covered by the procedure below. Define the population-minimal feasible repairs and their structural target by

ℛ≺⋆(P)={R:qR(P)≤0,qS(P)>0∀S≺R},Θ≺M​R(P)=⋃R∈ℛ≺⋆​(P)ΘR(P).\mathcal{R}^{\star}_{\prec}(P)=\{R:q_{R}(P)\leq 0,\ q_{S}(P)>0\ \forall S\prec R\},\qquad\Theta^{MR}_{\prec}(P)=\bigcup_{R\in\mathcal{R}^{\star}_{\prec}(P)}\Theta_{R}(P). (27)

When S≺RS\prec R means c⁡(S)<c⁡(R)c(S)<c(R), (27) reduces exactly to the scalar cost-minimum target. When repairs are deletion sets and S≺RS\prec R means S⊊RS\subsetneq R, it instead retains every inclusion-minimal feasible deletion.

Define

ℜ^n,≺={R:q¯R,n≤0,q¯S,n>0∀S≺R},Cn,≺PR=⋃R∈ℜ^n,≺Cn,R.\widehat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n,\prec}=\{R:\underline{q}_{R,n}\leq 0,\ \overline{q}_{S,n}>0\ \forall S\prec R\},\qquad C^{\mathrm{PR}}_{n,\prec}=\bigcup_{R\in\widehat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n,\prec}}C_{n,R}. (28)

This is again an existential projection of the coordinatewise feasibility-index box: RR is retained exactly when the box contains some vector for which RR is ≺\prec-minimal feasible. For recovery, let

aR​(P)=minS≺R⁡qS​(P),min⁡∅=+∞,a_{R}(P)=\min_{S\prec R}q_{S}(P),\qquad\min\varnothing=+\infty,

and define the repair-specific classification margin

δR≺​(P)={min⁡{−qR​(P),aR​(P)},R∈ℛ≺⋆​(P),max⁡{qR​(P),−aR​(P)},R∉ℛ≺⋆​(P),Δ≺​(P)=minR∈ℛ⁡δR≺​(P),\delta_{R}^{\prec}(P)=\begin{cases}\min\{-q_{R}(P),\,a_{R}(P)\},&R\in\mathcal{R}^{\star}_{\prec}(P),\\[2.0pt] \max\{q_{R}(P),\,-a_{R}(P)\},&R\notin\mathcal{R}^{\star}_{\prec}(P),\end{cases}\qquad\Delta_{\prec}(P)=\min_{R\in\mathcal{R}}\delta_{R}^{\prec}(P), (29)

where the minimum over an empty set of predecessors is +∞+\infty, so that aR​(P)=+∞a_{R}(P)=+\infty and −aR​(P)=−∞-a_{R}(P)=-\infty for a repair with no predecessor. A zero value records an unresolved feasibility or dominance boundary.

To make the meaning of this margin precise, for a deterministic vector v=(vR)R∈ℛv=(v_{R})_{R\in\mathcal{R}} define

ℳ≺(v)={R:vR≤0,vS>0∀S≺R},\mathcal{M}_{\prec}(v)=\{R:v_{R}\leq 0,\ v_{S}>0\ \forall S\prec R\},

and extend aRa_{R}, δR≺\delta_{R}^{\prec}, and Δ≺\Delta_{\prec} by replacing q⁡(P)q(P) with vv.

Proposition 1 (Exact minimality-stability radius).

For every v∈ℝ|ℛ|v\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{R}|} and every repair RR,

δR≺(v)=inf{∥w−v∥∞:𝟏{R∈ℳ≺(w)}≠𝟏{R∈ℳ≺(v)}}.\delta_{R}^{\prec}(v)=\inf\left\{\|w-v\|_{\infty}:\mathbf{1}\{R\in\mathcal{M}_{\prec}(w)\}\neq\mathbf{1}\{R\in\mathcal{M}_{\prec}(v)\}\right\}. (30)

Consequently,

Δ≺​(v)=inf{‖w−v‖∞:ℳ≺​(w)≠ℳ≺​(v)}.\Delta_{\prec}(v)=\inf\{\|w-v\|_{\infty}:\mathcal{M}_{\prec}(w)\neq\mathcal{M}_{\prec}(v)\}. (31)

Thus ℳ≺​(w)=ℳ≺​(v)\mathcal{M}_{\prec}(w)=\mathcal{M}_{\prec}(v) whenever ‖w−v‖∞<Δ≺​(v)\|w-v\|_{\infty}<\Delta_{\prec}(v), and for every ε>0\varepsilon>0 some ww with ‖w−v‖∞<Δ≺​(v)+ε\|w-v\|_{\infty}<\Delta_{\prec}(v)+\varepsilon has ℳ≺​(w)≠ℳ≺​(v)\mathcal{M}_{\prec}(w)\neq\mathcal{M}_{\prec}(v). The infima need not be attained, because feasibility is a weak inequality and predecessor infeasibility a strict one. If lower and upper feasibility-index endpoints satisfy maxR⁡max⁡{|q¯R−vR|,|q¯R−vR|}<Δ≺​(v)\max_{R}\max\{|\underline{q}_{R}-v_{R}|,|\overline{q}_{R}-v_{R}|\}<\Delta_{\prec}(v), then the interval rule {R:q¯R≤0,q¯S>0∀S≺R}\{R:\underline{q}_{R}\leq 0,\ \overline{q}_{S}>0\ \forall S\prec R\} equals ℳ≺​(v)\mathcal{M}_{\prec}(v). Conversely, no deterministic radius strictly larger than Δ≺​(v)\Delta_{\prec}(v) can guarantee this equality uniformly over endpoint vectors. For the cost order S≺RS\prec R iff c⁡(S)<c⁡(R)c(S)<c(R), whenever the model is repairable, Δ≺​{q⁡(P)}=Δ⁡(P)\Delta_{\prec}\{q(P)\}=\Delta(P).

For a minimal RR, status changes when vRv_{R} crosses above zero or a predecessor crosses from vS>0v_{S}>0 to vS≤0v_{S}\leq 0, giving distances −vR-v_{R} and aR​(v)a_{R}(v). For a nonminimal RR, entry requires correcting its own infeasibility, predecessor feasibility, or both, giving max⁡{vR,−aR​(v)}\max\{v_{R},-a_{R}(v)\}. Taking the finite minimum gives (31). If vR=0v_{R}=0 for a minimal repair, the radius is zero; using vS≥0v_{S}\geq 0 for predecessor infeasibility would be wrong because equality is feasible.

Replacing “cheaper” by “preceding” in the proof of Theorem 5 shows that, on the same event ℰn​(P)\mathcal{E}_{n}(P), Cn,≺PRC^{\mathrm{PR}}_{n,\prec} contains Θ≺M​R​(P)\Theta^{MR}_{\prec}(P), and that ℜ^n,≺=ℛ≺⋆​(Pn)\widehat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n,\prec}=\mathcal{R}^{\star}_{\prec}(P_{n}) with probability tending to one when Δ≺​(Pn)/ρn→∞\Delta_{\prec}(P_{n})/\rho_{n}\to\infty (Appendix, Corollary 5). With deletion-set repairs ordered by strict inclusion, this gives inference on the union over inclusion-minimal relaxations studied by Li et al. (2024), in the finite, compact setting of this paper. When the ranking itself is unsettled, one can fix a finite family of orders in advance and take unions: coverage, bandwise completeness, and recovery carry over, and the least separated order governs recovery (Appendix, Proposition 4). The local limits of Section 3 concern target membership and therefore apply to any of these targets.

4.4 Certified conclusions

Corollary 2 (Uniform certificates for repair-robust conclusions).

Let T⁡(P)T(P) denote ΘM​R​(P)\Theta^{MR}(P), Θ≺M​R​(P)\Theta^{MR}_{\prec}(P), or the order-robust target of Appendix S6, and let Cn⊆ΘC_{n}\subseteq\Theta be a measurable random closed set satisfying

lim infninfP∈𝒫ℙP{T(P)⊆Cn}≥1−α.\liminf_{n}\inf_{P\in\mathcal{P}}\mathbb{P}_{P}\{T(P)\subseteq C_{n}\}\geq 1-\alpha.

Fix continuous functionals g1,…,gL:Θ→ℝg_{1},\ldots,g_{L}:\Theta\to\mathbb{R} and use the conventions inf∅gℓ=+∞\inf_{\varnothing}g_{\ell}=+\infty and sup∅gℓ=−∞\sup_{\varnothing}g_{\ell}=-\infty. Then, with asymptotic probability at least 1−α1-\alpha uniformly in PP, [infCngℓ,supCngℓ]⊇[infT⁡(P)gℓ,supT⁡(P)gℓ][\inf_{C_{n}}g_{\ell},\sup_{C_{n}}g_{\ell}]\supseteq[\inf_{T(P)}g_{\ell},\sup_{T(P)}g_{\ell}] for every ℓ\ell simultaneously. Fix claim regions A1,…,AK⊆ΘA_{1},\ldots,A_{K}\subseteq\Theta for which {Cn⊆Ak}\{C_{n}\subseteq A_{k}\} is measurable. Then

lim supnsupP∈𝒫ℙP{∃k:Cn⊆Ak,T(P)⊈Ak}≤α.\limsup_{n}\sup_{P\in\mathcal{P}}\mathbb{P}_{P}\{\exists k:C_{n}\subseteq A_{k},\ T(P)\not\subseteq A_{k}\}\leq\alpha. (32)

Thus one entire-target event protects all prespecified universal conclusions read deterministically from CnC_{n}; no additional multiplicity correction is needed. If a claim is not certified, the procedure draws no conclusion about it.

The same logic applies to any fixed finite sensitivity family—for example, alternative cost rankings or tolerances—when one common event of probability at least 1−α1-\alpha implies target containment for every reported set, as it does for deterministic PR projections of that event. This does not justify choosing the sensitivity family after inspecting the data.

When containment in CnC_{n} is all that is used, this rule cannot be improved, and near a target-changing boundary a newly true claim is certified with probability at most Φ⁡(|h|​I−z1−α)\Phi(|h|\sqrt{I}-z_{1-\alpha}) along the experiment of Assumption 2; at α=0.05\alpha=0.05 and |h|​I=1|h|\sqrt{I}=1 this is about 0.260.26 (Appendix, Corollary 6).

5 The Statistical Price of Repair Uncertainty

Fix a candidate structural value θ\theta. In a regular local experiment, let

Y∼N⁡(h,Σ),Σ≻0.Y\sim N(h,\Sigma),\qquad\Sigma\succ 0.

Write Pu=N⁡(u,Σ)P_{u}=N(u,\Sigma) for the Gaussian law with mean uu. Let Kθ0K_{\theta}^{0} be the set of local means under which θ\theta remains in the post-relaxation target, and define

Kθ=cl⁡(Kθ0).K_{\theta}=\operatorname{cl}(K_{\theta}^{0}). (33)

Taking the closure is without loss: u↦Pu{Y∈G}u\mapsto P_{u}\{Y\in G\} is continuous for every measurable acceptance region GG, so honesty over Kθ0K_{\theta}^{0} and over KθK_{\theta} are equivalent. Define

dΣ​(h,Kθ)=infu∈Kθ(h−u)′​Σ−1​(h−u).d_{\Sigma}(h,K_{\theta})=\inf_{u\in K_{\theta}}\sqrt{(h-u)^{\prime}\Sigma^{-1}(h-u)}. (34)

An acceptance region GG is honest for θ\theta if Pu{Y∈G}≥1−αP_{u}\{Y\in G\}\geq 1-\alpha for every u∈Kθu\in K_{\theta}. For h∉Kθh\notin K_{\theta}, define the optimal retention probability

𝒜θ⋆(h)=infG:infu∈KθPu{Y∈G}≥1−αPh{Y∈G},\mathcal{A}_{\theta}^{\star}(h)=\inf_{G:\,\inf_{u\in K_{\theta}}P_{u}\{Y\in G\}\geq 1-\alpha}P_{h}\{Y\in G\},

where the infimum is over measurable acceptance regions. Thus 1−𝒜θ⋆​(h)1-\mathcal{A}_{\theta}^{\star}(h) is the largest rejection probability achievable at hh while retaining θ\theta with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha throughout its null membership region.

For closed convex KθK_{\theta}, let ΠKθΣ​(h)\Pi_{K_{\theta}}^{\Sigma}(h) denote the unique Mahalanobis projection of hh onto KθK_{\theta}. Given a supporting pair (aθ,κθ)(a_{\theta},\kappa_{\theta}), define the exposed-normal region

ℋθE​F={h∉Kθ:aθ′​ΠKθΣ​(h)=κθ,h−ΠKθΣ​(h)=λ​Σ​aθ​ for some ​λ>0}.\mathcal{H}_{\theta}^{EF}=\left\{h\notin K_{\theta}:\begin{array}[]{l}a_{\theta}^{\prime}\Pi_{K_{\theta}}^{\Sigma}(h)=\kappa_{\theta},\\ h-\Pi_{K_{\theta}}^{\Sigma}(h)=\lambda\Sigma a_{\theta}\text{ for some }\lambda>0\end{array}\right\}. (35)
Theorem 6 (Sharp Gaussian membership bound for convex regions).

Let h∉Kθh\notin K_{\theta}. If KθK_{\theta} is nonempty, closed, and convex, then

𝒜θ⋆​(h)=Φ⁡[z1−α−dΣ​(h,Kθ)].\mathcal{A}_{\theta}^{\star}(h)=\Phi\!\left[z_{1-\alpha}-d_{\Sigma}(h,K_{\theta})\right]. (36)

Suppose in addition that Kθ⊆{u:aθ′​u≤κθ}K_{\theta}\subseteq\{u:a_{\theta}^{\prime}u\leq\kappa_{\theta}\} for some aθ≠0a_{\theta}\neq 0. Then for every h∈ℋθE​Fh\in\mathcal{H}_{\theta}^{EF},

𝒯θ​(Y)=aθ′​Y−κθaθ′​Σ​aθ\mathcal{T}_{\theta}(Y)=\frac{a_{\theta}^{\prime}Y-\kappa_{\theta}}{\sqrt{a_{\theta}^{\prime}\Sigma a_{\theta}}} (37)

with acceptance rule 𝒯θ​(Y)≤z1−α\mathcal{T}_{\theta}(Y)\leq z_{1-\alpha} attains (36). For a finite nonconvex union of closed convex repair branches, the right side of (36) remains a lower bound, but equality need not hold unless one supporting half-space is valid over the entire union. With Kθ={−2,2}K_{\theta}=\{-2,2\}, Σ=1\Sigma=1, h=0h=0, and α=0.05\alpha=0.05, for example, the bound is 0.360.36 while the best honest test retains θ\theta with probability 0.670.67 (Appendix S8.3).

A plug-in version with uniformly consistent estimates of the supporting hyperplane and of Σ\Sigma attains the same bound uniformly on compact exposed-normal alternatives (Appendix).

I call (37) the exposed-face (EF) procedure; an exposed face is the intersection of a convex set with a supporting hyperplane. Theorem 6 is a sharp benchmark for convex Gaussian membership, not an efficiency claim for PR, whose finite-repair membership regions are generally nonconvex.

6 Resolution-Adaptive Inference

Once the feasibility margins dominate statistical resolution, Theorem 5 recovers the repair correspondence, and inference can adapt at the same point.

Split the sample into an independent pilot of size mnm_{n} and main sample of size Nn=n−mnN_{n}=n-m_{n}, indexed by ℐ1​n\mathcal{I}_{1n} and ℐ2​n\mathcal{I}_{2n}, with

mn→∞,mn/n→0.m_{n}\to\infty,\qquad m_{n}/n\to 0.

Let the pilot confidence level approach one, with α¯n↓0\bar{\alpha}_{n}\downarrow 0. Write q¯R,npil\underline{q}^{\mathrm{pil}}_{R,n} and q¯R,npil\overline{q}^{\mathrm{pil}}_{R,n} for the pilot feasibility bounds. A repair is definitely feasible if q¯R,npil≤0\overline{q}^{\mathrm{pil}}_{R,n}\leq 0 and definitely infeasible if q¯R,npil>0\underline{q}^{\mathrm{pil}}_{R,n}>0. These are the exact implications of the pilot interval, since feasibility is the weak inequality qR≤0q_{R}\leq 0. For a cost value aa, define

𝒟n(a)={R:c(R)=a,q¯R,npil≤0}.\mathscr{D}_{n}(a)=\{R:c(R)=a,\ \overline{q}^{\mathrm{pil}}_{R,n}\leq 0\}.

The layer aa is certified when every cheaper repair is definitely infeasible, every repair in the layer is classified as either definitely feasible or definitely infeasible, and 𝒟n​(a)≠∅\mathscr{D}_{n}(a)\neq\varnothing. At most one layer can be certified, because a certified layer contains a definitely feasible repair. The resolution-adaptive PR set, denoted CnRAC_{n}^{\mathrm{RA}}, uses the oracle procedure for a certified layer and PR otherwise. Formally, for a deterministic repair collection 𝒟\mathscr{D}, let Cn,𝒟O,MC_{n,\mathscr{D}}^{O,M} denote the chosen regular main-sample confidence procedure that treats 𝒟\mathscr{D} as known, and let Cn,mainPRC_{n,\mathrm{main}}^{\mathrm{PR}} denote PR built from the main sample. Define

CnRA={Cn,𝒟n​(a)O,M,if layer ​a​ is certified,Cn,mainPR,if certification fails.C_{n}^{\mathrm{RA}}=\begin{cases}C_{n,\mathscr{D}_{n}(a)}^{O,M},&\text{if layer }a\text{ is certified},\\ C_{n,\mathrm{main}}^{\mathrm{PR}},&\text{if certification fails}.\end{cases}

For comparison, let Cn,𝒟O,FC_{n,\mathscr{D}}^{O,F} denote the corresponding procedure based on the full sample and define the infeasible oracle benchmark

Cnoracle=Cn,ℛ⋆​(P)O,F,C_{n}^{\mathrm{oracle}}=C_{n,\mathcal{R}^{\star}(P)}^{O,F},

which knows the population-minimum repair correspondence. Write ℰnpil​(P)\mathcal{E}_{n}^{\mathrm{pil}}(P) for the analogue of ℰn​(P)\mathcal{E}_{n}(P) formed from the pilot bounds and ηmn,α¯npil​(P)\eta^{\mathrm{pil}}_{m_{n},\bar{\alpha}_{n}}(P) for the analogue of ηn​(P)\eta_{n}(P) in (21).

Assumption 5 (Resolution adaptation).

(i) Pilot. The pilot and main samples are independent, the pilot endpoints satisfy the requirements of Assumption 3, supP∈𝒫ℙP​{(ℰnpil​(P))c}≤α¯n+o⁡(1)\sup_{P\in\mathcal{P}}\mathbb{P}_{P}\{(\mathcal{E}_{n}^{\mathrm{pil}}(P))^{c}\}\leq\bar{\alpha}_{n}+o(1) with α¯n↓0\bar{\alpha}_{n}\downarrow 0, and ηmn,α¯npil\eta^{\mathrm{pil}}_{m_{n},\bar{\alpha}_{n}} satisfies (22) with a deterministic rate ρmn,α¯npil↓0\rho^{\mathrm{pil}}_{m_{n},\bar{\alpha}_{n}}\downarrow 0 in place of ρn\rho_{n}. (ii) Main-sample honesty. The fallback Cn,mainPRC_{n,\mathrm{main}}^{\mathrm{PR}} and, for every deterministic 𝒟\mathscr{D}, the oracle procedure Cn,𝒟O,MC_{n,\mathscr{D}}^{O,M} are functions of the main sample only; the fallback has asymptotic entire-target coverage at least 1−α1-\alpha uniformly over 𝒫\mathcal{P}, and Cn,𝒟O,MC_{n,\mathscr{D}}^{O,M} has it uniformly over {P∈𝒫:ℛ⋆​(P)=𝒟}\{P\in\mathcal{P}:\mathcal{R}^{\star}(P)=\mathscr{D}\} whenever that set is nonempty. (iii) Oracle equivalence. Along any sequence on which oracle equivalence is asserted, the full-sample and main-sample oracle procedures share an asymptotically linear representation and are locally Lipschitz in their inputs, as stated in Appendix S6.4.

Theorem 7 (Uniform honesty and oracle recovery).

Under Assumption 5(i)–(ii),

lim infninfP∈𝒫ℙP{ΘM​R(P)⊆CnRA}≥1−α.\liminf_{n}\inf_{P\in\mathcal{P}}\mathbb{P}_{P}\{\Theta^{MR}(P)\subseteq C_{n}^{\mathrm{RA}}\}\geq 1-\alpha. (38)

If, in addition, Pn∈𝒫P_{n}\in\mathcal{P} and

Δ⁡(Pn)/ρmn,α¯npil→∞,\Delta(P_{n})/\rho^{\mathrm{pil}}_{m_{n},\bar{\alpha}_{n}}\to\infty, (39)

then the pilot certifies ℛ⋆​(Pn)\mathcal{R}^{\star}(P_{n}) with probability tending to one. If Assumption 5(iii) also holds along this sequence, then

dH(CnRA,Cnoracle)=oPn(n−1/2).d_{H}(C_{n}^{\mathrm{RA}},C_{n}^{\mathrm{oracle}})=o_{P_{n}}(n^{-1/2}). (40)

In the fixed-dimensional IV class, where each oracle set is a finite union of intervals, Appendix S6.4 gives a primitive sufficient condition for part (iii): every population branch must have width κn\kappa_{n} with n​κn→∞\sqrt{n}\,\kappa_{n}\to\infty. Near branch collapse the condition fails: a branch can then be empty in the main sample and nonempty in the full sample, and the two sets differ by a fixed distance. The probability of this event is of order mn/n\sqrt{m_{n}/n}, so it vanishes, but slowly; in the Gaussian calculation of Appendix S6.4, with mn=n/log⁡nm_{n}=n/\log n, it is still about 0.100.10 at n=25,600n=25{,}600. Theorem 7 does not cover these sequences.

Because mn=o⁡(n)m_{n}=o(n) and α¯n↓0\bar{\alpha}_{n}\downarrow 0, the pilot resolves boundaries more slowly than the full sample: with mn=n/ℓnm_{n}=n/\ell_{n}, ℓn→∞\ell_{n}\to\infty, a regular pilot band has ρmn,α¯npil≍c1−α¯n​ℓn/n\rho^{\mathrm{pil}}_{m_{n},\bar{\alpha}_{n}}\asymp c_{1-\bar{\alpha}_{n}}\sqrt{\ell_{n}/n}, where c1−α¯nc_{1-\bar{\alpha}_{n}} is the simultaneous critical value, so certification requires n​Δ​(Pn)/(c1−α¯n​ℓn)→∞\sqrt{n}\,\Delta(P_{n})/(c_{1-\bar{\alpha}_{n}}\sqrt{\ell_{n}})\to\infty. This extra separation is the price of a vanishing pilot error probability. The same construction works under a finite partial order: the pilot then has to resolve only minimality status, not every feasibility sign (Appendix, Corollary 7).

7 Potentially Invalid Instruments

For the scalar linear IV specialization, some instruments may be invalid. The bounded-validity restriction below is in the spirit of plausibly exogenous sensitivity analysis (Conley et al., 2012); related work includes imperfect-instrument bounds (Nevo and Rosen, 2012), invalid-instrument selection (Kang et al., 2016), and falsification-adaptive IV analysis (Apfel and Windmeijer, 2024). The focus here is different: sampling uncertainty over which discrete repair is population-minimum and hence which repair-specific sets enter the post-relaxation target.

Fix P∈𝒫P\in\mathcal{P}, and write 𝔼P\mathbb{E}_{P} for expectation under PP. Let YY be the outcome, XX the endogenous regressor, CC a vector of included exogenous controls (including a constant), and Z1,…,ZJZ_{1},\ldots,Z_{J} the candidate instruments. After partialling out the controls, write

Y=β​X+U.Y=\beta X+U. (41)

For candidate instrument ZjZ_{j}, let tildes denote population residuals after projection on the included controls and set

πj=𝔼P​[Z~j​X~],|πj|≥π¯>0,\pi_{j}=\mathbb{E}_{P}[\widetilde{Z}_{j}\widetilde{X}],\qquad|\pi_{j}|\geq\underline{\pi}>0,

with just-identified estimand

βj=𝔼P​[Z~j​Y~]𝔼P​[Z~j​X~].\beta_{j}=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{P}[\widetilde{Z}_{j}\widetilde{Y}]}{\mathbb{E}_{P}[\widetilde{Z}_{j}\widetilde{X}]}. (42)

For each candidate validity claim, fix a prespecified tolerance rj≥0r_{j}\geq 0 and impose the sign-invariant bounded-validity restriction

|𝔼P​[Z~j​(Y~−β​X~)]||𝔼P​[Z~j​X~]|≤rj.\frac{|\mathbb{E}_{P}[\widetilde{Z}_{j}(\widetilde{Y}-\beta\widetilde{X})]|}{|\mathbb{E}_{P}[\widetilde{Z}_{j}\widetilde{X}]|}\leq r_{j}. (43)

Because 𝔼P​[Z~j​(Y~−β​X~)]=πj​(βj−β)\mathbb{E}_{P}[\widetilde{Z}_{j}(\widetilde{Y}-\beta\widetilde{X})]=\pi_{j}(\beta_{j}-\beta), (43) is equivalent to |β−βj|≤rj|\beta-\beta_{j}|\leq r_{j}. Thus validity claim jj contributes the interval Ij=[βj−rj,βj+rj]I_{j}=[\beta_{j}-r_{j},\beta_{j}+r_{j}].

Let the structural coefficient lie in fixed nondegenerate ex ante bounds

β∈[β¯,β¯],β¯<β¯.\beta\in[\underline{\beta},\overline{\beta}],\qquad\underline{\beta}<\overline{\beta}.

Index a repair RR by the set of abandoned validity claims, and let SRS_{R} denote the complementary set of retained instruments. Define

LR=max⁡{β¯,maxj∈SR⁡(βj−rj)},UR=min⁡{β¯,minj∈SR⁡(βj+rj)}.L_{R}=\max\left\{\underline{\beta},\max_{j\in S_{R}}(\beta_{j}-r_{j})\right\},\qquad U_{R}=\min\left\{\overline{\beta},\min_{j\in S_{R}}(\beta_{j}+r_{j})\right\}. (44)

With the conventions maxj∈∅⁡(βj−rj)=−∞\max_{j\in\varnothing}(\beta_{j}-r_{j})=-\infty and minj∈∅⁡(βj+rj)=+∞\min_{j\in\varnothing}(\beta_{j}+r_{j})=+\infty, deleting every candidate validity claim yields the structural-bound repair [β¯,β¯][\underline{\beta},\overline{\beta}], so the repair menu remains feasible even when all candidate instrument restrictions conflict. Then ΘR=[LR,UR]\Theta_{R}=[L_{R},U_{R}] when LR≤URL_{R}\leq U_{R}, and

qR=LR−UR.q_{R}=L_{R}-U_{R}. (45)

In the primitive form (10), each retained claim jj contributes the restrictions βj−rj−θ≤0\beta_{j}-r_{j}-\theta\leq 0 and θ−βj−rj≤0\theta-\beta_{j}-r_{j}\leq 0, and the structural bounds contribute β¯−θ≤0\underline{\beta}-\theta\leq 0 and θ−β¯≤0\theta-\overline{\beta}\leq 0.

7.1 Three-instrument benchmark

The tolerance rjr_{j} bounds the direct violation relative to the first-stage covariance, which makes the intervals comparable across instruments. Repair costs record which identifying claims are more costly to abandon. The benchmark uses equal costs only to normalize the ranking, not as a claim that all forms of invalidity are equally serious; Section 7.3 removes the dependence on costs altogether.

For the benchmark application, each abandoned validity claim has unit ex ante cost,

c⁡(R)=|R|.c(R)=|R|. (46)

When the structural bounds do not bind, a common tolerance rr gives exact algebra: a repair retaining one instrument has

qR=−2​r,q_{R}=-2r, (47)

a repair retaining instruments j,kj,k has qR=|βj−βk|−2​rq_{R}=|\beta_{j}-\beta_{k}|-2r, and the full three-instrument model has q∅=maxj<k⁡|βj−βk|−2​rq_{\varnothing}=\max_{j<k}|\beta_{j}-\beta_{k}|-2r. When the structural bounds do not bind, a one-instrument repair is feasible for every value of the coefficients, so there is nothing to estimate. I use these identities only when the simultaneous coefficient rectangle, enlarged by the tolerance, lies strictly inside (β¯,β¯)(\underline{\beta},\overline{\beta}), and the bounded formulas (44) otherwise; on the coverage event the identities then hold in population. A simultaneous band for each contrast βj−βk\beta_{j}-\beta_{k} gives bounds for |βj−βk|−2​r|\beta_{j}-\beta_{k}|-2r, and the maximum of the three gives a sandwich for q∅q_{\varnothing}. I call these the contrast-aware feasibility bounds. They are sharper than QRQ_{R} applied to marginal coefficient intervals and enter Assumption 3 directly. At r=0r=0 every one-instrument repair has qR=0q_{R}=0, so the strict predecessor rule in (16) rules out the delete-all repair. Values within rounding error of zero are treated as zero.

7.2 Influence functions and contrast-aware calibration

Let Y~\widetilde{Y}, X~\widetilde{X}, and Z~j\widetilde{Z}_{j} denote population residuals after projection on the included controls. Under iid sampling, a nonsingular second-moment matrix for the controls, finite moments sufficient for the sample projection coefficients, and the relevance bound above, the sample FWL ratio estimator is asymptotically linear with influence function

ψj​(W)=Z~j​(Y~−βj​X~)𝔼P​[Z~j​X~].\psi_{j}(W)=\frac{\widetilde{Z}_{j}(\widetilde{Y}-\beta_{j}\widetilde{X})}{\mathbb{E}_{P}[\widetilde{Z}_{j}\widetilde{X}]}. (48)

The Appendix derives this representation with the residualizing projections estimated.

For three instruments the empirical PR calibration uses the six-dimensional vector

V=(β1,β2,β3,β1−β2,β1−β3,β2−β3)′.V=(\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\beta_{3},\beta_{1}-\beta_{2},\beta_{1}-\beta_{3},\beta_{2}-\beta_{3})^{\prime}. (49)

Its influence vector is

Ψ=(ψ1,ψ2,ψ3,ψ1−ψ2,ψ1−ψ3,ψ2−ψ3)′.\Psi=(\psi_{1},\psi_{2},\psi_{3},\psi_{1}-\psi_{2},\psi_{1}-\psi_{3},\psi_{2}-\psi_{3})^{\prime}.

The six coordinates are linearly dependent, so the covariance matrix is singular; the studentized maximum needs only marginal variances bounded away from zero.

Proposition 2 (Uniform six-functional IV band).

Fix ϵ>0\epsilon>0, B<∞B<\infty, λC>0\lambda_{C}>0, π¯>0\underline{\pi}>0, and σ¯>0\underline{\sigma}>0. Let 𝒫I​V\mathcal{P}_{IV} be a fixed-dimensional iid class for W=(Y,X,Z1,Z2,Z3,C′)′W=(Y,X,Z_{1},Z_{2},Z_{3},C^{\prime})^{\prime} such that

supP∈𝒫I​V𝔼P​‖W‖4+ϵ≤B,infP∈𝒫I​Vλmin​𝔼P​[C​C′]≥λC,\sup_{P\in\mathcal{P}_{IV}}\mathbb{E}_{P}\|W\|^{4+\epsilon}\leq B,\qquad\inf_{P\in\mathcal{P}_{IV}}\lambda_{\min}\mathbb{E}_{P}[CC^{\prime}]\geq\lambda_{C},
infP∈𝒫I​Vminj≤3⁡|𝔼P​[Z~j​X~]|≥π¯,infP∈𝒫I​Vmink≤6⁡VarP⁡(Ψk)≥σ¯2,\inf_{P\in\mathcal{P}_{IV}}\min_{j\leq 3}|\mathbb{E}_{P}[\widetilde{Z}_{j}\widetilde{X}]|\geq\underline{\pi},\qquad\inf_{P\in\mathcal{P}_{IV}}\min_{k\leq 6}\operatorname{Var}_{P}(\Psi_{k})\geq\underline{\sigma}^{2},

where Ψk\Psi_{k} denotes coordinate kk of the influence vector just defined. Write V⁡(P)V(P) for the population value of (49). On samples for which the control residualization and all three FWL ratios are well defined and all six plug-in marginal variances are positive, let the critical value be the conditional (1−α)(1-\alpha) quantile of the Gaussian-multiplier maximum; otherwise use the full-band convention in the Appendix. Then

lim infninfP∈𝒫I​VℙP​{V⁡(P)​ is covered coordinatewise}≥1−α.\liminf_{n}\inf_{P\in\mathcal{P}_{IV}}\mathbb{P}_{P}\{V(P)\text{ is covered coordinatewise}\}\geq 1-\alpha.

The primitive IV bands and the contrast-aware feasibility-index sandwiches constructed from this event therefore satisfy Assumption 3 uniformly on 𝒫I​V\mathcal{P}_{IV}. The same holds when the conditional quantile is approximated by a number of multiplier draws that grows with nn.

The Appendix handles estimated residualization, singular Gaussian limits, and quantile continuity, the last through the anti-concentration inequality of Chernozhukov et al. (2015), which needs only marginal variances bounded away from zero; no denominator is truncated away from zero. The relevance bound is substantive: if a first stage approaches zero, the ratio experiment changes, and Proposition 2 no longer applies. Section 7.4 removes the bound.

7.3 Conclusions that hold over all tolerances and costs

The tolerance and the cost ranking are chosen by the researcher, and a reader may want to know whether a conclusion depends on either. With a common tolerance rj=rr_{j}=r, a single simultaneous band answers this for a whole range of tolerances and for every additive cost vector at once. Let JJ be the number of candidate validity claims (J=3J=3 in the application), let [ℓj,n,uj,n][\ell_{j,n},u_{j,n}] be the coordinates of the simultaneous band of Proposition 2 that correspond to βj\beta_{j}, and write Cn,r,wPRC^{\mathrm{PR}}_{n,r,w} for the PR set computed with tolerance rr and additive cost weights w=(w1,…,wJ)w=(w_{1},\ldots,w_{J}). For r≥0r\geq 0, define the conclusion envelope

Bn−​(r)=minj⁡ℓj,n−r,Bn+​(r)=maxj⁡uj,n+r.B_{n}^{-}(r)=\min_{j}\ell_{j,n}-r,\qquad B_{n}^{+}(r)=\max_{j}u_{j,n}+r. (50)

Fix a maximum tolerance r¯≥0\bar{r}\geq 0.

Corollary 3 (Tolerance- and cost-uniform IV conclusion envelope).

Use the contrast-aware feasibility bounds of Section 7.1. Suppose the deletion menu contains all subsets of the candidate validity claims and repair cost is additive,

cw​(R)=∑j∈Rwj,wj>0.c_{w}(R)=\sum_{j\in R}w_{j},\qquad w_{j}>0.

If

[Bn−​(r¯),Bn+​(r¯)]⊂(β¯,β¯),[B_{n}^{-}(\bar{r}),B_{n}^{+}(\bar{r})]\subset(\underline{\beta},\overline{\beta}), (51)

then for every r∈[0,r¯]r\in[0,\bar{r}] the structural bounds are nonbinding for every coefficient vector in the simultaneous rectangle, the delete-all repair is not PR-plausible for any strictly positive additive weight vector ww, and

Cn,r,wPR⊆[Bn−​(r),Bn+​(r)]∀r∈[0,r¯],w∈(0,∞)J.C_{n,r,w}^{\mathrm{PR}}\subseteq[B_{n}^{-}(r),B_{n}^{+}(r)]\qquad\forall r\in[0,\bar{r}],\quad w\in(0,\infty)^{J}. (52)

Consequently, any threshold τ<Bn−​(r)\tau<B_{n}^{-}(r) is certified as a universal lower conclusion, Cn,r,wPR⊂(τ,∞)C_{n,r,w}^{\mathrm{PR}}\subset(\tau,\infty), for every such ww; symmetrically, any τ>Bn+​(r)\tau>B_{n}^{+}(r) is certified as a universal upper conclusion. In particular, Bn−​(r¯)>0B_{n}^{-}(\bar{r})>0 implies positivity uniformly over the whole tolerance-and-cost class. On the common primitive coverage event, the corresponding population post-relaxation targets inherit all of these conclusions simultaneously.

The envelope separates uncertainty about the repair from uncertainty about the conclusion: the repair can remain unresolved while every value supported by every plausible minimum repair lies on the same side of a threshold. The realized Bn−​(r)B_{n}^{-}(r) is also a lower confidence bound, and a rounded value below it is a summary of that bound rather than a hypothesis chosen in advance. The contrast-aware bounds matter: with the canonical sandwich, a one-instrument repair cannot be shown feasible for small rr, the delete-all repair stays plausible, and PR returns the structural bounds. The proof is in the Appendix.

The theorem covers fixed zero first stages and every local-to-zero sequence in 𝒫W\mathcal{P}_{W}. It needs nondegenerate marginal score variances but not a nonsingular joint covariance matrix.

The boundary cases separate identification failure from refutation. If πj=γj=0\pi_{j}=\gamma_{j}=0, restriction jj is satisfied by every θ\theta and carries no identifying content. If πj=0\pi_{j}=0 but γj≠0\gamma_{j}\neq 0, every repair retaining jj is refuted. If all instruments retained by a repair have πj=γj=0\pi_{j}=\gamma_{j}=0, then that repair supports all of Θ\Theta. A minimum repair of this kind forces the post-relaxation target, and hence any honest entire-target confidence set, to include the structural bounds. A two-instrument example shows why the distinction matters. Let γ1=π1=1\gamma_{1}=\pi_{1}=1, r=0.2r=0.2, equal costs, and Θ=[−10,10]\Theta=[-10,10]. If (γ2,π2)=(0.5,0)(\gamma_{2},\pi_{2})=(0.5,0), the second claim is refuted, the minimum repair drops it, and the target is [0.8,1.2][0.8,1.2]. If (γ2,π2)=(0,0)(\gamma_{2},\pi_{2})=(0,0), the second instrument is merely irrelevant, the repair that keeps both claims is feasible at cost zero, and the target is again [0.8,1.2][0.8,1.2]. The sets agree but the diagnoses differ: in the first case the data say that a claim must be abandoned, in the second they say nothing about it. Ratio-based inference cannot tell the two apart, because both have π2=0\pi_{2}=0.

The set (58) checks the unreduced score γj−θ​πj\gamma_{j}-\theta\pi_{j} and never divides by π^j\widehat{\pi}_{j}. The common ν∈𝒦n\nu\in\mathcal{K}_{n} is essential: repair-by-repair extrema can use incompatible witnesses.

The rectangle 𝒦n\mathcal{K}_{n} treats γj\gamma_{j} and πj\pi_{j} as if they could move independently, which is what makes Theorem 8 valid even at πj=0\pi_{j}=0. When the first stages are nonzero but possibly weak, much of that freedom is wasted, because the restriction on θ\theta depends on (γj,πj)(\gamma_{j},\pi_{j}) only through the score γj−θ​πj\gamma_{j}-\theta\pi_{j}. Inverting the score directly gives a sharper set. For b∈ℝb\in\mathbb{R}, let ω^i​j​(b)=Z^j​i​(Y^i−b​X^i)\widehat{\omega}_{ij}(b)=\widehat{Z}_{ji}(\widehat{Y}_{i}-b\widehat{X}_{i}), where hats denote sample residuals after projection on the controls, let s^j2​(b)\widehat{s}_{j}^{2}(b) be the sample variance of ω^i​j​(b)\widehat{\omega}_{ij}(b) over ii, and for a critical value cc define

Fn,j={b∈ℝ:n​|n−1​∑i=1nω^i​j​(b)|≤c​s^j​(b)}.F_{n,j}=\Big\{b\in\mathbb{R}:\ \sqrt{n}\,\Big|n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\widehat{\omega}_{ij}(b)\Big|\leq c\,\widehat{s}_{j}(b)\Big\}. (60)

This is the Anderson–Rubin set for the ratio γj/πj\gamma_{j}/\pi_{j}; it may be an interval, a union of two half-lines, the whole line, or empty (Fieller, 1954). For a ratio vector b=(b1,…,bJ)b=(b_{1},\ldots,b_{J}), let T⁡(b)T(b) be the minimum-cost union of the sets [bj−rj,bj+rj]∩Θ[b_{j}-r_{j},b_{j}+r_{j}]\cap\Theta over the retained claims, with Θ\Theta for the delete-all repair, and define

Let 𝒫S\mathcal{P}_{S} satisfy the moment and control conditions of Theorem 8, with πj​(P)≠0\pi_{j}(P)\neq 0 for every jj but no lower bound on |πj​(P)||\pi_{j}(P)|, and suppose the covariance matrix of (Z~j​Y~,Z~j​X~)(\widetilde{Z}_{j}\widetilde{Y},\widetilde{Z}_{j}\widetilde{X}) has smallest eigenvalue at least σ¯2>0\underline{\sigma}^{2}>0 for every jj and P∈𝒫SP\in\mathcal{P}_{S}. At the true ratio the score has mean zero whatever the strength of the first stage, and the eigenvalue condition keeps the studentized score away from degeneracy even when βj​(P)\beta_{j}(P) diverges along a local-to-zero sequence, so each Anderson–Rubin statistic is asymptotically standard normal uniformly over 𝒫S\mathcal{P}_{S}; Bonferroni over the JJ instruments gives simultaneous coverage of β⁡(P)\beta(P), and the projection does the rest. 7.5 Breakdown tolerances

Corollary 3 and Proposition 3 also say how much invalidity a conclusion can withstand, in the spirit of the breakdown points of Masten and Poirier (2020). The tolerance has a direct economic reading. Write the income equation after partialling out the controls as Y~=β​X~+δj​Z~j+ej\widetilde{Y}=\beta\widetilde{X}+\delta_{j}\widetilde{Z}_{j}+e_{j} with 𝔼⁡(Z~j​ej)=0\mathbb{E}(\widetilde{Z}_{j}e_{j})=0, so that δj\delta_{j} is the direct effect of instrument jj on the outcome holding the endogenous regressor fixed, and let πjfs=𝔼⁡(Z~j​X~)/𝔼⁡(Z~j2)\pi_{j}^{\mathrm{fs}}=\mathbb{E}(\widetilde{Z}_{j}\widetilde{X})/\mathbb{E}(\widetilde{Z}_{j}^{2}) be its first-stage coefficient. Substituting this equation into (43) shows that the restriction is exactly |δj|≤rj​|πjfs||\delta_{j}|\leq r_{j}|\pi_{j}^{\mathrm{fs}}|. Since the reduced-form coefficient of ZjZ_{j} is βj​πjfs\beta_{j}\pi_{j}^{\mathrm{fs}}, an equivalent statement is that at most a fraction rj/|βj|r_{j}/|\beta_{j}| of the reduced-form association between ZjZ_{j} and the outcome is direct.

For a threshold τ\tau, a cost vector ww, and a maximum tolerance r¯\bar{r}, define the population breakdown tolerance

rτ,w⋆​(P)=sup{s∈[0,r¯]:Θr,wM​R​(P)⊂(τ,∞)​for every ​r∈[0,s]},r^{\star}_{\tau,w}(P)=\sup\Big\{s\in[0,\bar{r}]:\ \Theta^{MR}_{r,w}(P)\subset(\tau,\infty)\ \text{for every }r\in[0,s]\Big\},

with sup∅=−∞\sup\varnothing=-\infty, where Θr,wM​R​(P)\Theta^{MR}_{r,w}(P) is the target computed with common tolerance rr and additive costs ww. It is the largest common tolerance up to which every minimum-repair target lies above τ\tau. Because the minimum repair can change with rr, the condition is imposed for every smaller tolerance, not only at ss.

For a lower endpoint λn\lambda_{n} computed from the data, let r^τ,n​(λn)=min⁡{r¯,λn−τ}\widehat{r}_{\tau,n}(\lambda_{n})=\min\{\bar{r},\lambda_{n}-\tau\} if λn>τ\lambda_{n}>\tau and r^τ,n​(λn)=−∞\widehat{r}_{\tau,n}(\lambda_{n})=-\infty otherwise.

(i) Under the conditions of Proposition 2, use the contrast-aware feasibility bounds with all deletion subsets in the menu, and suppose (51) holds with probability approaching one uniformly in PP. Then

Add the JJ first-stage coefficients πjfs\pi_{j}^{\mathrm{fs}} to the functionals of Proposition 2, calibrate one simultaneous band for the enlarged vector, and let [π¯j,π¯j][\underline{\pi}_{j},\overline{\pi}_{j}] be its first-stage coordinates and λn+\lambda_{n}^{+} the smallest lower endpoint of its βj\beta_{j} coordinates. Put mj=min⁡{|π¯j|,|π¯j|}m_{j}=\min\{|\underline{\pi}_{j}|,|\overline{\pi}_{j}|\} if 0∉[π¯j,π¯j]0\notin[\underline{\pi}_{j},\overline{\pi}_{j}] and mj=0m_{j}=0 otherwise, and
