Section 9.7 reports the bounds for the application and translates them into direct effects of the historical instruments on income.

8 Monte Carlo Evidence

The simulations check four predictions of the theory. Seeds, complete tables, and Monte Carlo standard errors are in the replication package.

Hard selection at a boundary. In 300,000 replications of the scalar example of Section 1, hard selection covers the boundary value with probability 0.49990.4999 (s.e. 0.00090.0009), as the one-half limit predicts, and never covers the disconnected target. Along local alternatives the exposed-face procedure tracks the Gaussian retention bound of Theorem 6 to within simulation error.

Screening by PR. The second design has three instruments and seven instrument-retaining repairs, with coefficients and covariance calibrated to the published RST moments and the tolerance set at the boundary where two one-deletion repairs tie. The benchmark is the restricted union that always keeps all seven branches. At n=80n=80, hard selection covers the target in only 18.6%18.6\% of replications, while PR and the restricted union have the same average length. As nn grows, PR drops branches that the data rule out, and the ratio of its average length to that of the restricted union falls to 0.4660.466 at n=102,400n=102{,}400.

Adaptation. In a separated design with r=0.20r=0.20, the pilot certifies the correct repair correspondence with probability 0.9990.999 at n=102,400n=102{,}400, and the ratio of the average lengths of the adaptive and oracle sets is 1.0071.007. The scaled Hausdorff distance Nn​dH​(CnRA,Cnoracle)\sqrt{N_{n}}\,d_{H}(C_{n}^{\mathrm{RA}},C_{n}^{\mathrm{oracle}}) falls more slowly, from 3.23.2 at n=6,400n=6{,}400 to 1.31.3 at n=102,400n=102{,}400, so set-level equivalence is visibly slower than equivalence in length. A final experiment confirms that the strict predecessor rule excludes the delete-all repair under all seven cost rankings. Appendix S17 compares PR with the joint projection that exploits shared coefficients.

Weak identification. The last design mimics the application with a first stage that may be weak. Three independent instruments have ratios equal to the three estimates in Table 1; the first-stage FF statistics are about 2424 and 1515 for the ENG and EUR analogues and 9.9​λ29.9\lambda^{2} for the SM analogue, with λ∈{1,0.5,0.25,0.1}\lambda\in\{1,0.5,0.25,0.1\}, n∈{80,400}n\in\{80,400\}, and 2,000 replications per design (Appendix S14). I record whether the confidence event behind each procedure holds, which implies coverage of the whole target for every tolerance and cost vector. For the regular six-functional band this probability is 0.8650.865–0.9100.910 across designs and 0.8930.893 already at λ=1\lambda=1, where F≈10F\approx 10 as for SM in the data. For the score inversion of Proposition 3 it is 0.9400.940–0.9620.962. The reduced-form rectangle of Theorem 8 gives 0.9410.941–0.9550.955 at n=400n=400 but only 0.8900.890–0.9070.907 at n=80n=80, where the cross-products it studentizes are still far from normal. The robust procedures pay in informativeness. At λ=1\lambda=1 and n=80n=80 the score-inversion PR set at r=0.42r=0.42 is positive in 36% of replications, against 84% for the regular band; at λ=0.1\lambda=0.1 the figures are 2% and 23%. When the SM first stage is close to zero, its Anderson–Rubin set is unbounded, and the data cannot rule out ratio configurations in which SM is the only claim retained; the honest set then reaches the structural bound. Part of the regular band’s apparent informativeness in those designs comes from undercoverage. With equicorrelated instruments (correlation 0.50.5 or 0.80.8) the pattern is the same: the score inversion covers 0.9360.936–0.9630.963, the regular band 0.9040.904–0.9480.948, and the rectangle 0.8860.886–0.8980.898 at n=80n=80.

9 Institutions, Validity Restrictions, and Minimum Repair

9.1 Empirical design

The application revisits the institutions-and-development regressions of Rodrik et al. (2004). The structural equation is

Yi=μ0+β​𝑅𝑈𝐿𝐸i+μ1​𝐷𝐼𝑆𝑇𝐸𝑄i+Ui,Y_{i}=\mu_{0}+\beta\,\mathit{RULE}_{i}+\mu_{1}\mathit{DISTEQ}_{i}+U_{i}, (62)

where YY is log GDP per capita, 𝑅𝑈𝐿𝐸\mathit{RULE} is the rule-of-law index, and 𝐷𝐼𝑆𝑇𝐸𝑄\mathit{DISTEQ} is distance from the equator. There are three candidate validity claims, one for each historical instrument: log settler mortality (SM), the fraction of the population speaking English (ENG), and the fraction speaking a major European language (EUR). I use two samples. The main one is the 80-country sample in which all three instruments are observed (Section 9.2); combining the three on one sample is a new exercise rather than a replication of a particular RST column. The second is RST’s 140-country larger sample, in which settler mortality is missing and the two language instruments are jointly rejected (Section 9.4).

The goal is not a new preferred estimate of the effect of institutions but to ask whether the economic conclusion survives disagreement about where identification comes from. Settler mortality is the colonial-settlement instrument of Acemoglu et al. (2001); its data have themselves been disputed (Albouy, 2012). The language shares come from a different tradition and were used by RST in place of settler mortality in their larger sample, where RST reported overidentification concerns about them. The three instruments rest on different exclusion arguments, so dropping one rather than another is a substantive choice, and the 80-country sample puts the competing strategies on the same countries.

The question is whether the choice of which claim to discard changes the sign of β\beta, or an economically relevant lower bound on it, when the only maintained principle is to relax as little as the data require. A positive PR set means that every structural value supported by every band-compatible minimum repair is positive. It does not show that the exclusion restrictions hold, and it says nothing about a specification that treats every instrument as invalid.

The source file is matched to RST’s 80-country working-paper sample and checked against the published summary statistics before any inference is run. The common sample, covariance estimator, calibration, structural bounds [β¯,β¯]=[−10,10][\underline{\beta},\overline{\beta}]=[-10,10], tolerance grid, and cost-sensitivity schemes were recorded before the observation-level analysis; Appendix S16 gives the details.

Each abandoned claim has unit cost, as in (46). Equal costs encode the view that none of the three historical arguments is privileged a priori: the case for settler mortality rests on colonial disease environments and the case for the language shares on European settlement and legal transplants, and each has been disputed on its own terms. Readers who rank them differently can read off the cost-uniform results in Section 9.2 and the unequal-cost rows of Table 2. The tolerance rr is measured in units of the structural coefficient: by (43), it bounds the direct effect of the instrument on income relative to its first-stage effect on the rule-of-law index. The standard deviation of 𝑅𝑈𝐿𝐸\mathit{RULE} is about 0.850.85 in the 80-country sample, so a tolerance rr allows a direct effect equivalent to 0.85​r0.85r log points of income per standard deviation of the institutions measure. The reference value r=0.42r=0.42 was fixed from published moments before the observation-level file was opened (Appendix S16); since those moments come from the same sample, the choice is not independent of the outcome, which is why every conclusion is also stated for the whole range. It is about 39%39\% of the ENG estimate and 2121–22%22\% of the SM and EUR estimates. The tolerance is a sensitivity scale, not an estimate of the size of any exclusion violation.

9.2 Results for the 80-country sample

The common sample consists of the n=80n=80 countries with complete observations in the 2002 working-paper file posted by the authors. Summary statistics and first-stage regressions match the published extended-AJR sample, and every prespecified data check passes (Appendix S18). Table 1 reports the three just-identified estimates.

The estimates range from 1.071 (ENG) to 1.974 (EUR). Half the pairwise gaps, which are the common tolerances at which two instrument-specific intervals first meet, are 0.048 for SM and EUR, 0.403 for ENG and SM, and 0.451 for ENG and EUR, close to the values reconstructed from the published moments before the file was opened (Appendix S16).

The 95%95\% multiplier critical value for the six studentized coordinates is 2.5082.508. The implied simultaneous bands for the contrasts are [−1.845,0.234][-1.845,0.234] for ENG−-SM, [−2.021,0.216][-2.021,0.216] for ENG−-EUR, and [−1.413,1.219][-1.413,1.219] for SM−-EUR. All three contain zero, so the simultaneous contrast bands do not reject the joint validity restrictions at 5%5\%, even at r=0r=0. In this sample the model is not refuted; what the data cannot do is say whether, and how, it should be repaired. Section 9.4 turns to a sample in which the restrictions are rejected.

At r=0r=0 the point estimates call for two deletions and PR is [0.731,3.134][0.731,3.134]; at r=0.20r=0.20 they call for one deletion and PR is [0.531,3.334][0.531,3.334]; at the reference value r=0.42r=0.42 they still call for one deletion and PR is [0.311,3.554][0.311,3.554]; at r=0.50r=0.50 no deletion is needed and PR is [0.231,3.634][0.231,3.634]. At every tolerance in the grid the simultaneous band leaves all seven repairs that keep at least one instrument plausible, spread over cost layers 00, 11, and 22, so PR coincides with the restricted union over those seven repairs: with n=80n=80 the band screens out none of them. The literal union over the whole menu would include the delete-all repair and equal the structural bounds [−10,10][-10,10]. PR excludes that repair because a one-instrument repair is algebraically feasible and strictly cheaper under every positive additive cost vector. What the data deliver is a common sign: the whole PR set lies above zero, under the equal-cost ranking and under each of the seven prespecified alternatives (Appendix S18). The statement is uniform over the instrument-deletion repairs, tolerances, and cost vectors considered here. It does not say that the historical instruments satisfy their exclusion restrictions, and it does not say that β\beta is positive under unrestricted violations.

Corollary 3 turns these grid results into a statement about the continuum. For every common tolerance r∈[0,0.60]r\in[0,0.60] and every strictly positive additive cost vector, the PR set lies in [0.731−r, 3.134+r][0.731-r,\ 3.134+r]. The lower envelope is 0.3110.311 at r=0.42r=0.42 and 0.1310.131 at r=0.60r=0.60; rounded down, β>0.31\beta>0.31 and β>0.13\beta>0.13. These are summaries of a realized lower confidence bound, not thresholds fixed in advance. The sign conclusion is not sensitive to simulation error in the critical value: at r=0.60r=0.60 it would fail only if the critical value exceeded 2.97.

9.3 Weak identification

The results so far rely on a relevance bound, and the SM first stage (F=9.9F=9.9) is too weak to take that bound for granted. Proposition 3 removes it. With c=2.508c=2.508, the critical value used above, which exceeds the Bonferroni value z1−0.05/6=2.394z_{1-0.05/6}=2.394, the Anderson–Rubin sets (60) are [0.677,1.663][0.677,1.663] for ENG, [1.180,11.133][1.180,11.133] for SM, and [1.210,5.607][1.210,5.607] for EUR. All three are bounded intervals, and the ENG set lies inside the structural bounds, so the envelope part of the proposition applies: for every rr and every positive additive cost vector, the score-inversion PR set lies in [0.677−r, 10][0.677-r,\ 10]. The upper end is the structural bound because the SM set extends beyond it; with a weak instrument the data say little about how large the effect could be. The lower end is attained by the exact common-witness projection and stays positive for every tolerance up to 0.600.60, where it equals 0.0770.077. The positive sign therefore does not depend on the relevance bound.

The rectangle of Theorem 8 is valid in still greater generality, since it also allows πj=0\pi_{j}=0, but here it is much less informative. Its critical value is 2.5382.538, and the ratios γj/πj\gamma_{j}/\pi_{j} compatible with the rectangle range over [0.17,6.56][0.17,6.56] for ENG, [0.38,38.52][0.38,38.52] for SM, and [0.69,10.06][0.69,10.06] for EUR. The resulting PR set is positive only for r<0.17r<0.17. The reason is that the rectangle lets the reduced-form coefficient and the first stage move independently, whereas their estimation errors are strongly correlated; the score inversion uses that correlation. Figure 1(a) plots the three lower bounds against the tolerance.

9.4 A rejected model: the 140-country sample

Settler mortality is available for only 80 countries. For their larger sample RST rely on the two language instruments, and in that sample the maintained model is rejected by conventional tests. I use the n=140n=140 countries with complete data on income, rule of law, distance from the equator, the two language shares, and the integration variables of RST’s larger-sample regressions; the integration variables only define the sample. Settler mortality is defined only for former colonies, so the larger sample adds countries that were never colonized as well as former colonies without mortality data; the two samples differ in composition, and I do not compare magnitudes across them. This exercise was added during revision and was not part of the original analysis record.

The two just-identified estimates are 1.0281.028 for ENG (s.e. 0.1270.127, robust F=35.1F=35.1) and 1.6971.697 for EUR (s.e. 0.3340.334, F=17.4F=17.4). Both instruments are strong, so I use the regular implementation of Section 7, with the three functionals βENG\beta_{\mathrm{ENG}}, βEUR\beta_{\mathrm{EUR}}, and their difference in place of the six of Proposition 2. Hansen’s overidentification statistic is J=7.08J=7.08, with p=0.008p=0.008. A researcher who follows standard practice would conclude that at least one language instrument is invalid and report results with one of them dropped. Figure 1(b) and the lower panel of Table 2 show why the choice matters. Keeping only ENG gives the 95%95\% interval [0.78,1.28][0.78,1.28]; keeping only EUR gives [1.04,2.35][1.04,2.35]. They overlap only on [1.04,1.28][1.04,1.28], and the 2SLS interval under the rejected model, [0.96,1.58][0.96,1.58], excludes part of each.

PR does not choose. With the 95%95\% simultaneous band (critical value 2.2962.296), the contrast band [−1.415,0.077][-1.415,0.077] still contains zero: the JJ test examines the contrast alone, whereas PR must cover the two coefficients and the contrast together, so its band is wider and the maintained model cannot be excluded. PR is [0.74,2.46][0.74,2.46]. With the 90%90\% band (critical value 2.0052.005) the contrast band is [−1.320,−0.017][-1.320,-0.017], the maintained model is excluded for every r<0.009r<0.009, and at r=0r=0 the two one-deletion repairs are the only plausible ones; PR is their union, [0.77,2.37][0.77,2.37]. Neither level was fixed in advance, so I report both. At either level the lower end, 0.740.74 or 0.770.77, comes from the ENG branch and the upper end from the EUR branch, so a lower bound of about 0.750.75 holds whichever claim is dropped. Dropping one instrument rather than the other moves the upper bound by about one unit of β\beta. With r=0.42r=0.42, PR at 95%95\% is [0.32,2.88][0.32,2.88].

9.5 Comparison with simpler procedures

Table 2 puts PR next to the alternatives a referee would ask about, with every PR row computed from the same 95%95\% simultaneous band unless marked. Three comparisons stand out.

First, hard selection is narrower, but only because it ignores the repair problem. In the 80-country sample at r=0.42r=0.42, a researcher who keeps the repair favored by the point estimates (drop ENG, keep SM and EUR) and reports conventional intervals obtains [0.65,3.12][0.65,3.12]; PR gives [0.31,3.55][0.31,3.55]. In the 140-country sample the two hard choices give [0.78,1.28][0.78,1.28] and [1.04,2.35][1.04,2.35], and each excludes values supported by the other. Second, the union over every repair in the menu is uninformative, [−10,10][-10,10], because it keeps the repair that deletes every claim; the strict predecessor rule removes it without any statistical screening. Third, imposing that all repairs share the same coefficients, which Remark 1 shows can shrink PR in principle, changes nothing here: the exact shared-coefficient projection of the same band equals PR at both tolerances, to three decimals.

The last rows show that the cost ranking is a substantive input. In the 140-country sample at r=0r=0, PR with equal costs is [0.74,2.46][0.74,2.46]. If dropping the EUR claim is regarded as twice as costly as dropping the ENG claim, the repair that keeps only ENG is no longer minimal and PR becomes [0.93,2.46][0.93,2.46]; with the opposite ranking it is [0.74,1.32][0.74,1.32]. The lower bound moves from 0.740.74 to 0.930.93 and the upper bound from 2.462.46 to 1.321.32. The sign does not depend on the ranking; the magnitude does. A researcher who has a substantive reason to trust one language instrument more than the other should state it, because it matters.

The simplest serious competitor is the union of the one-instrument intervals from the same simultaneous band, [minj⁡ℓj,n−r,maxj⁡uj,n+r][\min_{j}\ell_{j,n}-r,\ \max_{j}u_{j,n}+r], which a careful researcher might report after deciding that any single instrument could be the valid one. With equal costs it coincides with PR in both samples (Table 2): with 80 countries the band screens out none of the seven instrument-retaining repairs, and the one-instrument branches contain all the others. In these data, then, PR does not deliver a narrower set; it delivers the justification for this one. It is the set that covers every minimum-repair target; it explains why the delete-all repair is excluded, since any single instrument within the tolerance restores feasibility at lower cost; and it carries the sign over every positive cost vector at once. The two sets separate as soon as the data certify that a cheaper repair is feasible. Hold the 80-country estimates and their correlations fixed and shrink the standard errors as if the sample had nn countries. At r=0.42r=0.42 the band first certifies that SM and EUR can be kept together at n≈255n\approx 255. The one-instrument repairs then stop being minimal, and the lower end of PR jumps to 0.870.87, against 0.460.46 for the union; at n=640n=640 the two are 1.091.09 and 0.530.53. This is a power calculation at fixed estimates, not evidence about the effect, but it shows where the minimum-repair rule pays: the lower end of the union is set by the ENG-only branch, and that branch drops out once two other instruments are known to agree. The unequal-cost rows of the 140-country sample give an instance in the actual data.

9.6 Economic magnitudes

The coefficient β\beta measures how log income responds to the rule-of-law index, a composite of survey and expert assessments, using historical variation to isolate exogenous differences. A positive β\beta says that the institutional quality captured by the index raises income on average; it does not say which reform would move the index or by how much. With that reading in mind, a convenient yardstick is the interquartile range. In the 80-country sample, moving from the 25th to the 75th percentile of the rule-of-law index is a change of 1.02 index points, while the interquartile gap in log income is 1.57. At r=0r=0, the PR lower bound implies that such a move raises log income by at least 0.750.75, about 48% of the income gap. At r=0.42r=0.42 the bound is 0.320.32 (20% of the gap), and at r=0.60r=0.60 it is 0.130.13 (9%). In standard-deviation units (sd⁡(𝑅𝑈𝐿𝐸)=0.85\mathrm{sd}(\mathit{RULE})=0.85), the bound at r=0.60r=0.60 is 0.1110.111 log point. For comparison, the SM point estimate alone would attribute 122% of the interquartile income gap to institutions and the ENG estimate 70%.

In the 140-country sample, the interquartile range of the index is 1.43 and the interquartile gap in log income is 2.11. The lower end of PR at r=0r=0 implies at least 1.051.05 log points, about 50% of the gap, and this bound does not depend on which language instrument is trusted. The upper end does. With only ENG, the upper confidence limit attributes at most 87% of the gap to institutions; with only EUR, the limit is 160%, more than the entire gap.

9.7 How much invalidity can the sign withstand?

Table 3 reports the lower confidence bounds of Corollary 4 for the sign of β\beta (τ=0\tau=0), together with their translation into direct effects. In the 80-country sample the regular band gives r^0,n=0.731\widehat{r}_{0,n}=0.731: every minimum-repair target is positive for every common tolerance up to this value and every positive additive cost vector. By the discussion before Corollary 4, and evaluating first-stage coefficients and βj\beta_{j} at their estimates, this tolerance allows up to 68% of the reduced-form association between English-language share and income to be direct, and up to 39% and 37% for settler mortality and the European-language share, all at once. In levels, the sign survives direct effects of 0.26, 0.23, and 0.20 log points of income per standard deviation of ENG, SM, and EUR. For comparison, the total reduced-form association of a one-standard-deviation change in each instrument with log income is 0.39, 0.60, and 0.53. Without a relevance bound the score-inversion bound is 0.677, only slightly smaller. The reduced-form rectangle gives 0.172, which corresponds to direct effects of about 0.06 log points per standard deviation; this is the price of allowing exactly zero first stages. In the 140-country sample the bound is 0.736 at the 95%95\% level and 0.773 at 90%90\%, so at the point estimates the sign survives direct effects of about 0.18 log points per standard deviation of the English-language share even though the two language instruments are jointly rejected.

These translations hold the first-stage coefficients at their estimates. The last two rows of Table 3 carry their uncertainty through, as in Remark 2: the band is recalibrated for the enlarged vector (critical value 2.6332.633 with nine functionals in the 80-country sample, 2.4752.475 with five in the larger sample), and each first stage is replaced by the end of its band closest to zero. With probability at least 95%95\%, β\beta is positive whenever the direct effects per standard deviation are below 0.13 for ENG, 0.04 for SM, and 0.05 for EUR in the 80-country sample, and below 0.10 and 0.06 for ENG and EUR in the larger sample. The guaranteed protection is much smaller than the point translations for SM and EUR. The SM first-stage band reaches −0.043-0.043, so the data cannot exclude a nearly irrelevant SM instrument, and a tolerance stated relative to a tiny first stage permits only a tiny direct effect. The English-language share is the only instrument whose first stage is precise enough to translate the tolerance into a substantial direct effect, about 0.13 log point per standard deviation in the 80-country sample and 0.10 in the larger one.

Taken together, the two samples support a lower bound and not much more. Institutions matter for income under every repair that the data cannot rule out, and the magnitude of that minimum effect is economically large when the instruments are held close to exact validity. Statements that institutions explain all of the cross-country income gap, or that a specific instrument identifies the effect, depend on which historical identifying argument one is willing to drop. These conclusions are conditional on the repair menu and on relaxing as little as the data require; if every historical claim could be abandoned at once, the answer would be the uninformative structural bounds.

10 Conclusion

When a model is refuted, several admissible relaxations may remain, and they may support different values of the parameter of interest. PR carries this uncertainty through a single simultaneous confidence statement. With a rectangular band on repair-specific primitives it reports exactly the post-relaxation targets that the band still permits, and it remains valid when the scientific ranking is a prespecified finite family of partial orders. How far the population sits from the nearest repair boundary determines whether the repair can be learned and how closely adaptive inference can approach the oracle.

PR is narrower than a worst case over every relaxation in the menu, which keeps dominated repairs, and broader than a single repair picked from the data, which can lose part of the target near a repair boundary.

The RST data illustrate both sides. In the 80-country sample the diagnosis and the economic conclusion do not resolve together: the data cannot tell which instrument claim, if any, should be dropped, yet every PR set is positive for r∈[0,0.60]r\in[0,0.60] and every strictly positive additive cost vector, with or without a first-stage relevance bound. In the 140-country sample the model is rejected, and the two repairs that remain give different answers about how large the effect of institutions is. PR keeps both, and the conclusion it supports is a lower bound that holds under either one.

Two extensions seem natural. The first is a menu that grows with the sample, for example when many moment inequalities can be dropped in blocks; the simultaneous band then has to be calibrated in high dimension, and Theorem 4 suggests that exploiting shared primitives becomes more important as the menu grows. The second is a ranking of repairs that is itself uncertain in a way that cannot be captured by a finite family of orders. Infinite repair menus, noncompact parameter spaces, and rankings estimated from the data remain outside the present theory.

Appendix S2 Proof of Theorem 1

S2.1 Lower semicontinuity

S6.1 PR under a fixed partial order

Corollary 5 (PR under a finite partial order).

Under the primitive repair setup and Assumption 3, on ℰn​(P)\mathcal{E}_{n}(P),

lim infninfP∈𝒫ℙP{Θ≺M​R(P)⊆Cn,≺PR}≥1−α.\liminf_{n}\inf_{P\in\mathcal{P}}\mathbb{P}_{P}\{\Theta^{MR}_{\prec}(P)\subseteq C^{\mathrm{PR}}_{n,\prec}\}\geq 1-\alpha.

If, in addition, Assumption 4 holds and Pn∈𝒫P_{n}\in\mathcal{P} satisfies

Δ≺​(Pn)/ρn→∞,\Delta_{\prec}(P_{n})/\rho_{n}\to\infty,

then

ℙPn{ℜ^n,≺=ℛ≺⋆(Pn)}→1.\mathbb{P}_{P_{n}}\{\widehat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n,\prec}=\mathcal{R}^{\star}_{\prec}(P_{n})\}\to 1.

The confidence set Cn,≺PRC^{\mathrm{PR}}_{n,\prec} is a measurable random closed set under the same measurability conditions as CnPRC_{n}^{\mathrm{PR}}.

With deletion-set repairs ordered by strict inclusion, Corollary 5 covers the union over all inclusion-minimal data-consistent relaxations. When the repair-specific sets coincide with those used in the misspecification-robust bound of Li et al. (2024), this yields a uniformly valid confidence region for the finite-repair version of that target under the simultaneous-band conditions. The qualification matters: the argument here uses a compact finite-repair representation and does not cover all of the infinite-dimensional or noncompact models allowed in their identification analysis.

Once the repair correspondence and structural target are specified, the local impossibility results do not depend on how the ranking was represented. In particular, Theorem 2 and Corollary 1 apply after replacing ℛ⋆\mathcal{R}^{\star} by ℛ≺⋆\mathcal{R}^{\star}_{\prec}, while Theorem 3 and the Gaussian bound of Theorem 6 operate directly on target membership and therefore apply with ΘM​R\Theta^{MR} replaced by Θ≺M​R\Theta^{MR}_{\prec}. What is ranking-specific is the population cost geometry in Theorem 1 and the scalar-layer certification rule; Section S6.5 gives the corresponding adaptive certification rule for a partial order.

S6.2 Robustness to a prespecified family of repair orders

The scientific ranking of repairs may itself be unsettled. Let 𝔒\mathfrak{O} be a nonempty finite collection of strict partial orders on ℛ\mathcal{R}, fixed before the data are observed. Define

ℛ𝔒⋆(P)=⋃≺∈𝔒ℛ≺⋆(P),Θ𝔒M​R(P)=⋃≺∈𝔒Θ≺M​R(P),\mathcal{R}^{\star}_{\mathfrak{O}}(P)=\bigcup_{\prec\in\mathfrak{O}}\mathcal{R}^{\star}_{\prec}(P),\qquad\Theta^{MR}_{\mathfrak{O}}(P)=\bigcup_{\prec\in\mathfrak{O}}\Theta^{MR}_{\prec}(P), (S.1)

and

ℜ^n,𝔒=⋃≺∈𝔒ℜ^n,≺,CPRn,𝔒=⋃≺∈𝔒CPRn,≺.\widehat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n,\mathfrak{O}}=\bigcup_{\prec\in\mathfrak{O}}\widehat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n,\prec},\qquad C^{\mathrm{PR}}_{n,\mathfrak{O}}=\bigcup_{\prec\in\mathfrak{O}}C^{\mathrm{PR}}_{n,\prec}. (S.2)

This target is robust to uncertainty over the prespecified orders; it does not select an order from the data.

Proposition 4 (Order-robust post-relaxation projection).

Under the primitive repair setup and Assumption 3, on ℰn​(P)\mathcal{E}_{n}(P),

ℛ𝔒⋆​(P)⊆ℜ^n,𝔒,Θ𝔒M​R​(P)⊆Cn,𝔒PR.\mathcal{R}^{\star}_{\mathfrak{O}}(P)\subseteq\widehat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n,\mathfrak{O}},\qquad\Theta^{MR}_{\mathfrak{O}}(P)\subseteq C^{\mathrm{PR}}_{n,\mathfrak{O}}.

Consequently, Cn,𝔒PRC^{\mathrm{PR}}_{n,\mathfrak{O}} is a measurable random closed set and has uniform asymptotic entire-target coverage at least 1−α1-\alpha. For a primitive array ff, let T≺​(f)T_{\prec}(f) be the union of the ≺\prec-minimal feasible repair targets generated by ff. Under the canonical rectangular band,

Cn,𝔒PR=⋃f∈𝔅nrep⋃≺∈𝔒T≺(f).C^{\mathrm{PR}}_{n,\mathfrak{O}}=\bigcup_{f\in\mathfrak{B}_{n}^{\mathrm{rep}}}\ \bigcup_{\prec\in\mathfrak{O}}T_{\prec}(f). (S.3)

Thus the inclusion-minimality and claim-certification equivalence in Theorem 4 also hold for the order-robust target. Define

Δ𝔒(P)=min≺∈𝔒Δ≺(P).\Delta_{\mathfrak{O}}(P)=\min_{\prec\in\mathfrak{O}}\Delta_{\prec}(P). (S.4)

If Assumption 4 holds and Δ𝔒​(Pn)/ρn→∞\Delta_{\mathfrak{O}}(P_{n})/\rho_{n}\to\infty, then

ℙPn{ℜ^n,≺=ℛ≺⋆(Pn) for every ≺∈𝔒}→1,\mathbb{P}_{P_{n}}\{\widehat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n,\prec}=\mathcal{R}^{\star}_{\prec}(P_{n})\text{ for every }\prec\in\mathfrak{O}\}\to 1,

and hence ℜ^n,𝔒=ℛ𝔒⋆​(Pn)\widehat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n,\mathfrak{O}}=\mathcal{R}^{\star}_{\mathfrak{O}}(P_{n}) with probability tending to one.

Finiteness of 𝔒\mathfrak{O} is substantive. It permits one common simultaneous event, allows the two unions in (S.3) to commute, and makes simultaneous recovery depend on the least separated candidate order. Estimated or growing order families are not covered.

S6.3 Sharpness of conclusion certificates

Corollary 6 (Sharpness and local resolution of conclusion certificates).

Let A⊆ΘA\subseteq\Theta be a fixed claim region for which {Cn⊆A}\{C_{n}\subseteq A\} is measurable, let C⊆ΘC\subseteq\Theta be nonempty and compact, and let g:Θ→ℝg:\Theta\to\mathbb{R} be continuous. If the only information about a nonempty compact target is T⊆CT\subseteq C, then C⊆AC\subseteq A is necessary and sufficient to guarantee T⊆AT\subseteq A for every such target, and minC⁡g,maxC⁡g\min_{C}g,\max_{C}g are the sharp corresponding functional envelopes. Moreover, if Tn=T⁡(Pn)T_{n}=T(P_{n}), sn>0s_{n}>0 is deterministic, dH​(Cn,Tn)=OPn​(sn)d_{H}(C_{n},T_{n})=O_{P_{n}}(s_{n}), and κA​(Pn)=dist⁡(Tn,Θ∖A)\kappa_{A}(P_{n})=\dist(T_{n},\Theta\setminus A) satisfies κA​(Pn)/sn→∞\kappa_{A}(P_{n})/s_{n}\to\infty, then ℙPn{Cn⊆A}→1\mathbb{P}_{P_{n}}\{C_{n}\subseteq A\}\to 1. Along the LAN experiment of Assumption 2, if θ†∈T⁡(Pn,0)∖A\theta^{\dagger}\in T(P_{n,0})\setminus A and boundary entire-target coverage is at least 1−α1-\alpha, then for every fixed hh,

lim supnPn,h{Cn⊆A}≤Φ(|h|I−z1−α).\limsup_{n}P_{n,h}\{C_{n}\subseteq A\}\leq\Phi\!\left(|h|\sqrt{I}-z_{1-\alpha}\right). (S.5)

If T⁡(Pn,h)⊆AT(P_{n,h})\subseteq A eventually, this bounds the probability of correctly certifying the newly true repair-robust claim. The same statements hold for the partial-order target.

The local bound is an information limit, not a peculiarity of PR. For example, at α=.05\alpha=.05 and |h|​I=1|h|\sqrt{I}=1, its upper bound is about 0.2600.260; it reaches one half only at |h|​I=z.95|h|\sqrt{I}=z_{.95}.

Remark 3 (Why the proof avoids a generic derivative of the feasibility map).

The canonical map QRQ_{R} can be nonsmooth because minimizers move and active inequalities change, and a direct feasibility index such as the IV gap LR−URL_{R}-U_{R} can be nonsmooth for the same reason. PR does not differentiate either object. For the canonical construction, monotonicity of QRQ_{R} propagates the primitive band into a feasibility sandwich; for sharper implementations, Assumption 3 allows that sandwich to be established directly. Standard directional methods remain available when a local derivative can be estimated reliably, but they are not needed for the entire-target coverage argument.

The pilot need not resolve the feasibility sign of every repair in order to resolve partial-order minimality. Define the definitely minimal and definitely nonminimal collections

𝒟n,≺pil\displaystyle\mathscr{D}_{n,\prec}^{\mathrm{pil}} ={R:q¯R,npil≤0,q¯S,npil>0∀S≺R},\displaystyle=\left\{R:\overline{q}_{R,n}^{\mathrm{pil}}\leq 0,\ \underline{q}_{S,n}^{\mathrm{pil}}>0\ \forall S\prec R\right\}, (S.6)
𝒩n,≺pil\displaystyle\mathscr{N}_{n,\prec}^{\mathrm{pil}} ={R:q¯R,npil>0​ or ​q¯S,npil≤0​ for some ​S≺R}.\displaystyle=\left\{R:\underline{q}_{R,n}^{\mathrm{pil}}>0\text{ or }\overline{q}_{S,n}^{\mathrm{pil}}\leq 0\text{ for some }S\prec R\right\}. (S.7)

The correspondence is partial-order certified when 𝒟n,≺pil≠∅\mathscr{D}_{n,\prec}^{\mathrm{pil}}\neq\varnothing, 𝒟n,≺pil∩𝒩n,≺pil=∅\mathscr{D}_{n,\prec}^{\mathrm{pil}}\cap\mathscr{N}_{n,\prec}^{\mathrm{pil}}=\varnothing, and their union is ℛ\mathcal{R}. Cn,≺RA\displaystyle C_{n,\prec}^{\mathrm{RA}} ={Cn,𝒟n,≺pilO,M,if partial-order certification succeeds,Cn,main,≺PR,otherwise,\displaystyle=\begin{cases}C_{n,\mathscr{D}_{n,\prec}^{\mathrm{pil}}}^{O,M},&\text{if partial-order certification succeeds},\\ C_{n,\mathrm{main},\prec}^{\mathrm{PR}},&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}
Cn,≺oracle\displaystyle C_{n,\prec}^{\mathrm{oracle}} =Cn,ℛ≺⋆​(P)O,F.\displaystyle=C_{n,\mathcal{R}^{\star}_{\prec}(P)}^{O,F}.

For the next result, impose the partial-order analogue of Assumption 5: part (i) is unchanged; in part (ii), replace ΘM​R\Theta^{MR}, ℛ⋆\mathcal{R}^{\star}, and the PR fallback by Θ≺M​R\Theta^{MR}_{\prec}, ℛ≺⋆\mathcal{R}^{\star}_{\prec}, and Cn,main,≺PRC_{n,\mathrm{main},\prec}^{\mathrm{PR}}, respectively; and in part (iii), replace ℛ⋆​(Pn)\mathcal{R}^{\star}(P_{n}) by ℛ≺⋆​(Pn)\mathcal{R}^{\star}_{\prec}(P_{n}) throughout. These replacements are the only changes.

Corollary 7 (Partial-order resolution adaptation).

Under parts (i)–(ii) of the partial-order analogue of Assumption 5,

lim infninfP∈𝒫ℙP{Θ≺M​R(P)⊆Cn,≺RA}≥1−α.\liminf_{n}\inf_{P\in\mathcal{P}}\mathbb{P}_{P}\{\Theta^{MR}_{\prec}(P)\subseteq C_{n,\prec}^{\mathrm{RA}}\}\geq 1-\alpha.

If, in addition, Pn∈𝒫P_{n}\in\mathcal{P} and

Δ≺​(Pn)/ρmn,α¯npil→∞,\Delta_{\prec}(P_{n})/\rho^{\mathrm{pil}}_{m_{n},\bar{\alpha}_{n}}\to\infty,

then partial-order certification succeeds and returns ℛ≺⋆​(Pn)\mathcal{R}^{\star}_{\prec}(P_{n}) with probability tending to one. Under part (iii) of the partial-order analogue,

dH(Cn,≺RA,Cn,≺oracle)=oPn(n−1/2).d_{H}(C_{n,\prec}^{\mathrm{RA}},C_{n,\prec}^{\mathrm{oracle}})=o_{P_{n}}(n^{-1/2}).

The pilot is designed to resolve minimality status; it need not determine every feasibility sign. With the weak feasibility boundary treated exactly, the two status sets above are the maximal deterministic conclusions obtainable from the rectangular pilot feasibility-index box: RR is definitely minimal precisely when its own upper endpoint is nonpositive and every predecessor’s lower endpoint is positive, and it is definitely nonminimal precisely when its own lower endpoint is positive or some predecessor’s upper endpoint is nonpositive. A nonminimal repair may therefore lie on its own feasibility boundary and still be safely excluded when a scientifically preferred predecessor is known feasible. Proposition 1 shows that Δ≺\Delta_{\prec} is exactly the deterministic perturbation radius governing that distinction.

Appendix S7 Proofs for the finite partial-order extension

This section proves Proposition 1, Corollary 5, and Corollaries 2 and 6. Let ≺\prec be a fixed strict partial order on the finite repair menu and define

ℛ≺⋆(P)={R:qR(P)≤0,qS(P)>0∀S≺R}.\mathcal{R}^{\star}_{\prec}(P)=\{R:q_{R}(P)\leq 0,\ q_{S}(P)>0\ \forall S\prec R\}.

On the simultaneous primitive event, Lemma 1 gives

q¯R,n≤qR​(P)≤q¯R,n∀R.\underline{q}_{R,n}\leq q_{R}(P)\leq\overline{q}_{R,n}\qquad\forall R. (S.8)

For arbitrary deterministic coordinatewise feasibility intervals, the finite-sample projection rule is exact: RR can be ≺\prec-minimal feasible for some vector in the rectangle if and only if q¯R≤0\underline{q}_{R}\leq 0 and q¯S>0\overline{q}_{S}>0 for every S≺RS\prec R. The strict predecessor inequality is essential: if q¯S=0\overline{q}_{S}=0, predecessor SS is feasible throughout the rectangle and RR can never be minimal. Theorem 4 strengthens this coordinate statement for the canonical construction by projecting the entire primitive rectangle into the structural target.

S7.1 Exact perturbation geometry

For a deterministic vector v=(vR)R∈ℛv=(v_{R})_{R\in\mathcal{R}}, write

ℳ≺(v)={R:vR≤0,vS>0∀S≺R},aR(v)=minS≺RvS,\mathcal{M}_{\prec}(v)=\{R:v_{R}\leq 0,\ v_{S}>0\ \forall S\prec R\},\qquad a_{R}(v)=\min_{S\prec R}v_{S},

with min⁡∅=+∞\min\varnothing=+\infty. Fix RR.

If R∈ℳ≺​(v)R\in\mathcal{M}_{\prec}(v), then vR≤0v_{R}\leq 0 and aR​(v)>0a_{R}(v)>0. A perturbation changes RR from minimal to nonminimal precisely by making either its own coordinate strictly positive or at least one predecessor coordinate nonpositive. The infimum sup-norm distances to those two events are, respectively, −vR-v_{R} and aR​(v)a_{R}(v). Hence the distance to their union is

min⁡{−vR,aR​(v)}=δR≺​(v).\min\{-v_{R},a_{R}(v)\}=\delta_{R}^{\prec}(v).

If vR=0v_{R}=0, the first distance is zero but is not attained: for every ε>0\varepsilon>0, setting wR=εw_{R}=\varepsilon and leaving all other coordinates fixed changes the status with ‖w−v‖∞=ε\|w-v\|_{\infty}=\varepsilon. Hence δR≺​(v)=0\delta_{R}^{\prec}(v)=0, and therefore Δ≺​(v)=0\Delta_{\prec}(v)=0 whenever any minimal repair lies on its own feasibility boundary. If vR<0v_{R}<0, the analogous infimum −vR-v_{R} is also generally not attained because leaving feasibility requires the strict inequality wR>0w_{R}>0.

Now suppose R∉ℳ≺​(v)R\notin\mathcal{M}_{\prec}(v). Three cases remain. If vR>0v_{R}>0 and aR​(v)>0a_{R}(v)>0, entering the minimality region requires only moving vRv_{R} to a nonpositive value, so the infimum distance is vRv_{R}. If vR≤0v_{R}\leq 0 and aR​(v)≤0a_{R}(v)\leq 0, entering the minimality region requires moving every nonpositive predecessor coordinate strictly above zero; the infimum sup-norm distance is −aR​(v)-a_{R}(v). If vR>0v_{R}>0 and aR​(v)≤0a_{R}(v)\leq 0, both changes are necessary, so the infimum distance is

max⁡{vR,−aR​(v)}.\max\{v_{R},-a_{R}(v)\}.

These cases give max⁡{vR,−aR​(v)}=δR≺​(v)\max\{v_{R},-a_{R}(v)\}=\delta_{R}^{\prec}(v) on the nonminimal region; repairs without predecessors reduce to ordinary feasibility. This proves the repair-specific identity (30).

The correspondence changes if and only if the minimality status of at least one repair changes. Since the menu is finite, the distance to that finite union of status-changing sets is the minimum of the repair-specific distances. Therefore

inf{‖w−v‖∞:ℳ≺​(w)≠ℳ≺​(v)}=minR⁡δR≺​(v)=Δ≺​(v).\inf\{\|w-v\|_{\infty}:\mathcal{M}_{\prec}(w)\neq\mathcal{M}_{\prec}(v)\}=\min_{R}\delta_{R}^{\prec}(v)=\Delta_{\prec}(v).

maxR⁡max⁡{|q¯R−vR|,|q¯R−vR|}<Δ≺​(v).\max_{R}\max\{|\underline{q}_{R}-v_{R}|,|\overline{q}_{R}-v_{R}|\}<\Delta_{\prec}(v).

Appendix S9 Proofs of Theorem 7 and Corollary 7

S9.1 Safe certification

For a cost value aa, the rule of Section 6 forms

𝒟n(a)={R:c(R)=a,q¯R,npil≤0}\mathscr{D}_{n}(a)=\{R:c(R)=a,\ \overline{q}^{\mathrm{pil}}_{R,n}\leq 0\}

and certifies layer aa only when every cheaper repair has q¯S,npil>0\underline{q}^{\mathrm{pil}}_{S,n}>0, every repair in the layer has either q¯R,npil≤0\overline{q}^{\mathrm{pil}}_{R,n}\leq 0 or q¯R,npil>0\underline{q}^{\mathrm{pil}}_{R,n}>0, and 𝒟n​(a)\mathscr{D}_{n}(a) is nonempty. On a valid pilot band, a repair with nonpositive upper feasibility bound is truly feasible, whereas a repair with positive lower bound is truly infeasible. Therefore, if layer aa is certified, all cheaper repairs are truly infeasible and the definitely feasible repairs in layer aa are exactly all feasible repairs in that layer. Since at least one is feasible, a=c⋆​(P)a=c^{\star}(P) and 𝒟n​(a)=ℛ⋆​(P)\mathscr{D}_{n}(a)=\mathcal{R}^{\star}(P). A boundary repair with qR​(P)=0q_{R}(P)=0 can be certified feasible only in the special but logically valid case in which its pilot upper endpoint is exactly zero; otherwise a band that straddles zero correctly prevents certification of its status. Thus the rule is maximally decisive given only the rectangular pilot feasibility-index intervals, rather than imposing an artificial strict-feasibility requirement.

Let Gn​(P)=ℰnpil​(P)G_{n}(P)=\mathcal{E}_{n}^{\mathrm{pil}}(P) be the valid-pilot event. By the pilot-validity part of the resolution-adaptation assumption,

supP∈𝒫ℙP​{Gn​(P)c}≤α¯n+o⁡(1).\sup_{P\in\mathcal{P}}\mathbb{P}_{P}\{G_{n}(P)^{c}\}\leq\bar{\alpha}_{n}+o(1).

Let Pn∈𝒫P_{n}\in\mathcal{P} and write ρnpil=ρmn,α¯npil\rho_{n}^{\mathrm{pil}}=\rho^{\mathrm{pil}}_{m_{n},\bar{\alpha}_{n}}. By pilot validity and Δ⁡(Pn)/ρnpil→∞\Delta(P_{n})/\rho_{n}^{\mathrm{pil}}\to\infty, the fixed-MM repair-recovery argument above gives

S9.5 Partial-order certification and oracle recovery

On the valid pilot event, R∈𝒟n,≺pilR\in\mathscr{D}_{n,\prec}^{\mathrm{pil}} implies that RR is feasible and every predecessor is infeasible, hence R∈ℛ≺⋆​(P)R\in\mathcal{R}^{\star}_{\prec}(P); while R∈𝒩n,≺pilR\in\mathscr{N}_{n,\prec}^{\mathrm{pil}} is nonminimal because either RR is infeasible or a predecessor is feasible. These two status conditions are exact for a Cartesian product of scalar pilot intervals: if neither holds, two vectors inside the same box can be chosen so that RR is minimal under one and nonminimal under the other. Thus, whenever the two status sets partition ℛ\mathcal{R} and the definitely minimal set is nonempty, safe certification returns exactly ℛ≺⋆​(P)\mathcal{R}^{\star}_{\prec}(P).

Uniform honesty follows from the same conditioning argument as in the scalar-cost case. On the valid pilot event, the procedure either falls back to Cn,main,≺P​RC_{n,\mathrm{main},\prec}^{PR} or uses the independent main-sample oracle-subset procedure indexed by the true deterministic collection ℛ≺⋆​(P)\mathcal{R}^{\star}_{\prec}(P). The main-sample-honesty part of the partial-order analogue bounds either failure probability by α+o⁡(1)\alpha+o(1) uniformly. Because ℛ\mathcal{R} is finite, the maximum oracle remainder vanishes, while pilot failure contributes α¯n+o⁡(1)\bar{\alpha}_{n}+o(1). Hence

lim infninfP∈𝒫ℙP{Θ≺M​R(P)⊆Cn,≺R​A}≥1−α.\liminf_{n}\inf_{P\in\mathcal{P}}\mathbb{P}_{P}\{\Theta^{MR}_{\prec}(P)\subseteq C_{n,\prec}^{RA}\}\geq 1-\alpha.

If Δ≺​(Pn)/ρmn,α¯npil→∞\Delta_{\prec}(P_{n})/\rho^{\mathrm{pil}}_{m_{n},\bar{\alpha}_{n}}\to\infty, the same fixed-MM argument used above gives ηmn,α¯npil​(Pn)≤Δ≺​(Pn)/3\eta^{\mathrm{pil}}_{m_{n},\bar{\alpha}_{n}}(P_{n})\leq\Delta_{\prec}(P_{n})/3 with probability tending to one. The exact stability-radius proposition then classifies every repair’s minimality status correctly, so certification returns ℛ≺⋆​(Pn)\mathcal{R}^{\star}_{\prec}(P_{n}). On that event put 𝒟n=ℛ≺⋆​(Pn)\mathscr{D}_{n}=\mathcal{R}^{\star}_{\prec}(P_{n}). Part (iii) of the partial-order analogue provides the same common primitive representation and common Hausdorff-Lipschitz map Γn,𝒟n\Gamma_{n,\mathscr{D}_{n}} as in the scalar proof. dH(Cn,≺R​A,Cn,≺oracle)=oPn(n−1/2).d_{H}(C_{n,\prec}^{RA},C_{n,\prec}^{\mathrm{oracle}})=o_{P_{n}}(n^{-1/2}).

Appendix S16 Sample construction and the analysis record

The data version matters. The 2002 working paper reports an 80-country extended-AJR sample, whereas the published 2004 article uses 79 countries after sample revisions (Rodrik et al., 2002; Rodrik et al., 2004). The source file is matched to the 80-country profile, and its summary statistics are checked against the published values, before any inference is run.

Before running the observation-level analysis, I recorded the common sample, the HC0 heteroskedasticity-robust covariance estimator, the six-functional multiplier calibration and its seed, the structural bounds [β¯,β¯]=[−10,10][\underline{\beta},\overline{\beta}]=[-10,10], the tolerance grid, the benchmark ranking, and seven cost-sensitivity schemes. The reference tolerance r=0.42r=0.42 had already been chosen from published moments for the same sample (Section S16.1), so this record is not an independent preregistration.

S16.1 Reconstruction from published moments

Before opening the observation-level file, I reconstructed the just-identified estimates from the second moments reported for the 80-country working-paper sample:

(βENG,βSM,βEUR)=(1.073,1.879,1.973),(r12,r23,r13)=(0.403,0.047,0.450),(\beta_{\mathrm{ENG}},\beta_{\mathrm{SM}},\beta_{\mathrm{EUR}})=(1.073,1.879,1.973),\qquad(r_{12},r_{23},r_{13})=(0.403,0.047,0.450),

where instruments are indexed 1=ENG1=\mathrm{ENG}, 2=SM2=\mathrm{SM}, 3=EUR3=\mathrm{EUR} and rj​k=|βj−βk|/2r_{jk}=|\beta_{j}-\beta_{k}|/2 is the common tolerance at which the intervals centered on instruments jj and kk first intersect. As rr increases, the point-estimate minimum repair therefore moves from two deletions, to a single one-deletion repair, to two tied one-deletion repairs, and finally to no deletion. S16.2 The 140-country sample in detail

Table S3 collects the 140-country results of Section 9.4 and reports how many repairs PR retains at each level.

Appendix S17 Shared primitives: rectangular versus joint projection

Remark 1 shows that canonical PR can be strictly larger than the union of targets compatible with a band whose coordinates enter several repairs. This section measures how large the difference is in repeated samples. There are two just-identified coefficients β1,β2\beta_{1},\beta_{2}, estimated independently with normal errors of standard deviations 0.250.25 and 0.0150.015, so the first instrument is much less precise than the second, as in the remark. The menu contains the repair that keeps both instruments (cost 00) and the two repairs that keep one (cost 11); r=0.1r=0.1 and Θ=[−1,2]\Theta=[-1,2]. The band is the Bonferroni rectangle with critical value 2.2412.241. Canonical PR treats the two coordinates as separate primitives of each repair. The joint projection collects ΘM​R​(b)\Theta^{MR}(b) over all points bb of the band; on the band event it contains the target, and it is contained in canonical PR. Both sets are computed exactly on a grid of mesh 10−310^{-3}, with 2,000 replications per design.

Both procedures attain the nominal level. The joint projection is strictly smaller in at most 19% of replications, and its mean length is never below 99% of that of PR. The gain appears only when the imprecise coefficient can be small enough to make the full-information repair feasible while the precise one pins the other end of the band, the configuration of the remark. Under the rectangular information set PR is sharp (Theorem 4); this design suggests that what is lost by ignoring shared primitives is small, while the joint projection has a cost that grows with the number of repairs.

S18.1 Prespecified deletion-cost sensitivity

Equal costs are the primary specification. Before the observation-level analysis I also recorded the seven distinct positive cost vectors with entries in {1,2}\{1,2\}, up to scale. Table S6 lists the repairs that PR keeps at r=0.42r=0.42 under each of them.

Across the seven rankings, the lower endpoint of the PR set at r=0.42r=0.42 ranges from 0.311 to 0.393 and the upper endpoint from 3.345 to 3.554, so every ranking gives the same sign (positive).

The same holds for all 63 combinations of reporting tolerance and cost ranking; the smallest lower endpoint among them is 0.231. All of these statements follow from the same six-functional band, so they hold simultaneously and need no separate calibration.

Corollary 3 extends the table to a continuum. The lower endpoints of the simultaneous coefficient bands are ENG=0.731, SM=0.828, EUR=0.813; the largest upper endpoint is 3.134. After expansion by the maximum prespecified tolerance r¯=0.60\bar{r}=0.60, the envelope is [0.131,3.734][0.131,3.734], which lies strictly inside [−10,10][-10,10]. The sign is therefore positive for every r∈[0,0.60]r\in[0,0.60] and every strictly positive additive deletion-cost vector.

The replication package contains the complete tolerance grid for all seven cost vectors. The cost vectors were fixed before the observation-level estimates were computed.

This section gives the details behind Section 9.3. The calculation was added after the main observation-level analysis and was not part of the original analysis record.

Let a^j=n−1​∑iZ~j​i​Y~i\widehat{a}_{j}=n^{-1}\sum_{i}\widetilde{Z}_{ji}\widetilde{Y}_{i} and p^j=n−1​∑iZ~j​i​X~i\widehat{p}_{j}=n^{-1}\sum_{i}\widetilde{Z}_{ji}\widetilde{X}_{i}, with residuals taken after partialling out a constant and DISTEQ. A value bb is retained for instrument jj when

|a^j−b​p^j|≤cn​s^j​(b),\left|\widehat{a}_{j}-b\widehat{p}_{j}\right|\leq\frac{c}{\sqrt{n}}\,\widehat{s}_{j}(b), (S.13)

where s^j2​(b)\widehat{s}_{j}^{2}(b) is the sample variance of Z~j​i​(Y~i−b​X~i)\widetilde{Z}_{ji}(\widetilde{Y}_{i}-b\widetilde{X}_{i}). This is the set (60) of Proposition 3: the ratio inversion of Fieller (1954), which tests a structural value through the unreduced moment, as in Anderson and Rubin (1949), rather than by dividing by an estimated first stage.

I use c=2.508c=2.508, the six-functional multiplier critical value of the main analysis. Squaring (S.13) gives a quadratic inequality in bb, which is solved without assuming that the solution is bounded; intervals, pairs of half-lines, the whole line, and the empty set are all possible. In the RST sample all three solutions are bounded intervals (Table S7).

The ENG set lies inside the structural bounds [−10,10][-10,10], so the envelope part of Proposition 3 applies: for every common tolerance rr and every strictly positive additive cost vector, the score-inversion PR set is contained in [0.677−r, 10][0.677-r,\,10].
